result.question: Web accessibility patterns as design-time decisions, not code fixes — narrow scope, four tightly related topics: (1) which ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) patterns encode designer decisions rather than developer ones — disclosure vs accordion vs tabs, dialog vs alertdialog, combobox vs listbox vs select, menu vs menubar vs toolbar, treegrid vs grid vs table — and the visual/interaction commitments each pattern obliges (keyboard model, focus behavior, visible state); (2) the "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule and the five rules of ARIA use — named cases where a native element or layout change is correct instead, the measured harm bad ARIA causes screen reader users, and WebAIM Million data on ARIA correlating with higher detected error rates; (3) focus management on route change and view transitions in SPAs — where focus should go, role of skip links and page-title announcement, how the View Transitions API interacts with focus and prefers-reduced-motion, and the known failure of focus being lost to document body; (4) live regions and aria-live for asynchronous results — polite vs assertive, role=status vs role=alert, aria-atomic and aria-relevant, the requirement that the live region exist in the DOM before injection, and documented cross-screen-reader failure modes across NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver. Primary/authoritative sources only (W3C WAI APG, ARIA spec, WebAIM and the WebAIM Million, TPGi/Deque where W3C is silent).
result.summary: One query per named sub-topic (APG pattern selection, the anti-ARIA rules plus WebAIM Million evidence, SPA route-change focus and View Transitions, live-region semantics and failures), each anchored with the exact spec terminology and source names so search returns w3.org/webaim.org/tpgi/deque rather than blog restatements. A fifth query adds the empirical counterweight — ARIA-AT interoperability test reports showing where APG patterns themselves fail under real NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver — which is what turns pattern choice into a design-time risk decision.

angles.rationale: Pulls the W3C ARIA-in-HTML rules plus the WebAIM Million's quantified finding that pages using ARIA average substantially more detected errors — the empirical harm claim the question asks to verify.

angles.rationale: Covers the accepted correct behavior on navigation, the documented body-focus failure, and the newer View Transitions interaction with focus and reduced-motion — where W3C is thin and TPGi/Deque/WICG explainers carry the detail.

angles.rationale: Surfaces aria-at.w3.org test reports and TPGi/Deque testing writeups showing where APG patterns and live regions actually fail per screen reader — the evidence that makes pattern choice a design risk decision, not a compliance checkbox.

results.title: Prototype Testing for Accessible Client-Side Routing — Marcy Sutton
results.snippet: The primary-source study behind almost every later recommendation on SPA route focus. Sutton built competing prototypes (focus to a wrapper element, focus to the h1, ARIA live-region announcement only, skip-link-takes-focus) and tested them with screen reader users, rather than asserting a pattern from spec reading. Directly answers the sub-question 'where should focus go' with evidence, and names the failure mode where nothing is announced and focus remains on the stale link from the previous view. Also documents a non-obvious defect: focus-to-wrapper on a large element caused mobile Chrome to scroll to the element's middle, cutting off the heading text — the kind of visual/interaction consequence that makes this a design-time decision, not a code fix.

results.title: What we learned from user testing of accessible client-side routing techniques with Fable Tech Labs — Gatsby
results.snippet: The written-up results of the same Fable Tech Labs user testing round, framed as findings rather than methodology. Establishes the now-accepted answer: shift focus to the h1 on each route change, which simultaneously resets reading position to the top of the new view and causes the page title to be announced — provided the h1 is actually descriptive, which is a content/design commitment. Useful as the citable outcome for 'what is the accepted correct behavior on route change,' and it explicitly weighs heading-focus against wrapper-focus and against live-region-only announcement, which is the design fork the question is asking about.

results.title: Accessibility Tips in Single-Page Applications — Deque
results.snippet: Deque technical writeup, one of the source types the question explicitly accepts where W3C is silent (WCAG and the APG say nothing normative about client-side route focus). Enumerates the places focus is routinely lost in SPAs — route change, item deletion, modal close, expanding/collapsing detail records — which is the general class the 'focus falls to document body' failure belongs to. Also covers the skip-link-receives-focus-on-route-change variant and the requirement that the skip link's label state what activating it will do.

results.title: View Transition API — MDN Web Docs
results.snippet: Authoritative platform reference for the newest half of the question, where no W3C WAI guidance exists yet. Covers the same-document (SPA) startViewTransition flow and the cross-document variant, and the accessibility caveats that matter here: during the transition both old and new content are captured/present, which produces loss of reading position, focus confusion, and unreliable live-region announcement timing. Also the reference point for the prefers-reduced-motion interaction — the standard guidance is to wrap ::view-transition animations in a reduced-motion media query or skip the transition in JS, since the browser does not universally neutralize the animation for you.

results.title: Animating Page and View Transitions with Accessibility in Mind
results.snippet: One of the few writeups that treats View Transitions and focus management as a single problem instead of separate ones — covers ordering the focus move relative to the transition's ready/finished promises, and gating the animation on prefers-reduced-motion while keeping the focus move unconditional (the focus reset is an accessibility requirement, the animation is decoration). Practitioner-grade rather than normative, so treat it as implementation detail, but it fills the gap the W3C and MDN leave on how the two mechanisms sequence.

results.title: SPA Accessibility — focus not reset when route changed · remix-run/react-router Discussion #9863
results.snippet: Documents the body-focus failure as it actually manifests in a widely used router rather than in the abstract: after a client-side navigation the router replaces the DOM subtree containing the focused link, focus falls back to document.body, and the screen reader announces nothing while the virtual cursor is stranded. Useful as evidence that this is a default-behavior problem — routers do not reset focus for you, so the framework silence is why the design decision has to be made explicitly. Long-running discussion, so weigh the maintainer replies over the drive-by suggestions.

results.title: Patterns | ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) | W3C WAI
results.snippet: The pattern index itself is the design-time selection artifact: each of the ~27 patterns (Accordion, Disclosure, Tabs, Dialog/Modal, Alert Dialog, Combobox, Listbox, Menu/Menubar, Toolbar, Grid, Table, Treegrid) carries a one-line 'what this is for' summary, and every pattern page is structured identically — About This Pattern, Examples, Keyboard Interaction, WAI-ARIA Roles/States/Properties. That structure is the point for this question: choosing a pattern name commits you to its Keyboard Interaction table and its required visible states. Start here to see the full choice set side by side before drilling into an individual pattern.

results.title: Combobox Pattern | APG | WAI | W3C
results.snippet: Directly answers combobox vs listbox vs native select. APG states the behavioral difference as a design decision, not a code one: in a combobox popup the user can arrow through choices and press Escape to close without changing prior input, whereas 'navigating among options in a single-select listbox immediately changes its value, and Escape does not provide an undo mechanism.' Also defines the Select-Only Combobox as 'functionally similar to an HTML select element', and APG has deprecated the Collapsible Dropdown Listbox in favor of it. Specifies the focus commitment: DOM focus stays on the combobox while aria-activedescendant points at the focused option inside the listbox/grid/tree popup.

results.title: Grid (Interactive Tabular Data and Layout Containers) Pattern | APG | WAI | W3C
results.snippet: The clearest W3C statement of grid vs table vs treegrid as a design-time fork. Grid is 'a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys, such as arrow keys, Home, and End' — i.e. choosing grid commits you to arrow-key cell navigation and a single tab stop. The companion Table pattern (w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/table/) states a WAI-ARIA table 'is not an interactive widget. Thus, its cells are not focusable or selectable', so each widget inside a table becomes its own tab stop — the opposite keyboard contract. Treegrid (w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/treegrid/) adds row expand/collapse to the grid contract for 'a hierarchical data grid consisting of tabular information that is editable or interactive'.

results.title: Dialog (Modal) Pattern | APG | WAI | W3C
results.snippet: Covers dialog vs alertdialog and the focus obligations both incur. APG: 'The alertdialog role is designed specifically for dialogs that divert users' attention to a brief, important message' — an interruption that acquires a response (confirmations, error acknowledgements), which is why it is announced like an alert while a plain dialog is not. The pattern page specifies the non-negotiable behaviors a designer signs up for: initial focus placement inside the dialog, focus trapped while open, Escape closes, and focus returned to the invoking element on close — plus accessible-name requirements via aria-labelledby/aria-label.

results.title: Menu and Menubar Pattern | APG | WAI | W3C
results.snippet: Defines the menu/menubar contract: an application-style command menu modeled on desktop GUI menus, with arrow-key navigation inside a single tab stop, submenu parents carrying aria-haspopup plus aria-expanded true/false, and type-ahead. This is the pattern most often mis-chosen at design time for site navigation (which is a list of links, not a menu). Pair with the Toolbar pattern (w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/toolbar/) — 'a container for grouping a set of controls, such as buttons, menubuttons, or checkboxes' — where controls stay active rather than being commands that dismiss the container, and with Developing a Keyboard Interface (w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/practices/keyboard-interface/) for the roving-tabindex vs aria-activedescendant decision every composite pattern forces.

results.title: Disclosure (Show/Hide) Pattern | APG | WAI | W3C
results.snippet: The lightest of the three show/hide patterns and the correct default: a single button whose aria-expanded is true when content is visible and false when hidden, with optional aria-controls — no arrow keys, no roving focus, content sits in the normal tab order. Contrast with Accordion (w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/accordion/), 'a vertically stacked set of interactive headings' where headers are wrapped in heading elements, panels use role=region/aria-labelledby, and Up/Down Arrow between headers is optional; and with Tabs (w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/tabs/), where the tablist is one tab stop, Left/Right Arrow moves between tabs, and you must decide automatic vs manual activation. Escalating from disclosure to accordion to tabs is a design decision that adds keyboard and state obligations each step.

results.title: W3C ARIA specification — aria-live property (and live region attributes)
results.snippet: The normative source for topic (4). Confirmed by fetch: "Assistive technology will only convey CHANGES to a live region, not the initial contents. Authors SHOULD create a rendered but empty live region as early as possible (such as on page load), and then modify the content when changes are expected to be announced." This is the exact spec sentence behind the "live region must exist in the DOM before content is injected" rule — and note it is a SHOULD in the spec, not a MUST, so the hard requirement widely repeated in blogs is implementation convention hardened by AT behavior, not normative prose. Same section carries aria-atomic (present whole region vs changed portion) and aria-relevant (additions/removals/text/all) definitions, plus the implicit live-region behavior of role=alert (assertive, atomic, announces on render) and role=status (polite, atomic, conveys changes).

results.title: Live Region Support — Adrian Roselli (updated Jan 2026)
results.snippet: The current primary-testing matrix for cross-screen-reader failure modes, and the single most useful source where W3C is silent. Tested NVDA/Firefox (2023.1–2025.3.2), JAWS/Chrome (114–144), VoiceOver/Safari macOS+iOS (12.6–26.2), plus Narrator, Orca, TalkBack. Documented failures: JAWS and Narrator collapse assertive into polite (announce "at first break"); VoiceOver macOS drops polite regions during read-all, losing content on Braille displays; JAWS and Narrator do not prepend "alert" to role=alert messages; Orca does not announce role=alert content at all; NVDA Braille shows "alert" with no message; Narrator fails to announce <output> (role=status) across all tested versions. Key design-time takeaway: no live region announces while hidden — hidden, aria-hidden, and display:none all suppress it, so the region has to be rendered, not just present.

results.title: Screen reader support for ARIA live regions — TPGi
results.snippet: TPGi's longitudinal support testing, explicitly one of the source types the research question asks for. Establishes that live region behavior is a browser+AT pair property, not a markup property: e.g. adding role=status forces some ATs to honor a polite region that they otherwise ignore, while making no difference to VoiceOver on iOS; iOS Safari historically only fired the test case when the region was assertive. Useful for the design-time argument that choosing polite vs assertive and status vs alert is a commitment to a set of real announcement behaviors that vary by AT, not a semantic label.

results.title: ARIA19: Using ARIA role=alert or Live Regions to Identify Errors — W3C WAI (WCAG 2.2 Techniques)
results.snippet: W3C's own sufficient technique connecting live regions to asynchronous/validation results, i.e. the normative-adjacent guidance for when role=alert is the correct choice for error output versus a polite status region. Provides the conformance framing (which SC it satisfies) plus tests, which is what turns "use a live region" from a code detail into a design-time commitment: if the design shows an inline error or an async result, the announcement path is a conformance obligation, not an enhancement.

results.title: ARIA live regions — MDN Web Docs
results.snippet: Fills in the implementation convention layer the spec leaves loose: the practical requirement that the region be empty on page load or when first added to the DOM, the exception that role=alert does not need to be pre-registered before it is populated, and the aria-atomic / aria-relevant combinations (aria-relevant="additions removals" etc.) with worked examples. Good for separating "spec says SHOULD" from "what actually announces" — but it is a secondary restatement, so treat spec-anchored claims as coming from w3c.github.io/aria.

results.title: Live Region Playground — Deque University
results.snippet: Deque's interactive testbed for every combination of aria-live (off/polite/assertive), role (alert/status/log/timer), aria-atomic, aria-relevant, and injection method. Relevant as the empirical instrument behind the failure-mode claims: it lets a designer or reviewer verify what a chosen politeness/atomicity combination actually announces in NVDA/JAWS/VoiceOver rather than trusting the attribute names. Named-source tier (Deque) per the question's sourcing rules.

results.title: Assistive Technology Support Tables | ARIA Authoring Practices Guide | W3C WAI
results.snippet: The authoritative W3C page that turns APG pattern choice into a measurable risk decision. Defines the two metrics ARIA-AT publishes per AT+browser combination — "Must-Have Behaviors" (absence *blocks* access, e.g. a radio's name and checked state never conveyed) and "Should-Have Behaviors" (absence *impedes*, e.g. position-in-set / set-size). Explicitly instructs authors that when must-have support is below 100% they should compare support across multiple implementation examples of the same pattern, do their own multi-AT testing, and NOT code around AT bugs. This is the direct empirical counterpart to topic (1): choosing disclosure vs accordion vs tabs, or combobox vs listbox, is choosing a different measured support percentage, not just a different keyboard model. Also the source of the framing that support summaries are attached to individual APG example pages, so a designer can check a pattern before committing to it.

results.title: Live Region Support — Adrian Roselli (Jan 2026)
results.snippet: The most current empirical cross-screen-reader matrix for topic (4), and the strongest evidence that aria-live semantics are not honored uniformly. Documented failures: JAWS + Chrome treats *all* live regions as polite regardless of aria-live value and fails to prepend "alert" for role=alert; NVDA + Firefox announces polite regions at the first break rather than at sentence end, and role=alert interrupts then re-announces the interrupted content; VoiceOver/macOS makes aria-live="polite" behave assertively on Braille displays with content loss, double-announces <output>, and drops polite regions entirely during read-all; TalkBack flipped from assertive (13.1) to polite (16.0.0). One universal failure across every combination tested: a hidden live region never announces, whether hidden via `hidden`, `aria-hidden`, or `display:none`. Notably does not test aria-atomic/aria-relevant — itself a signal about how little of that surface is verified.

results.title: Why are my live regions not working? — TetraLogical
results.snippet: The primary documented case for the "live region must exist in the DOM before content is injected" requirement in topic (4), with the spec rationale and the tested failure table. Live regions expose *changes*, so a region rendered already-populated is generally not announced; the working pattern is to prime an empty container, then inject after a setTimeout. Per-AT deviations recorded: NVDA and JAWS announce pre-populated content only for role=alert and only inconsistently; VoiceOver announces pre-populated role=alert with an earcon; JAWS + Firefox announces *all* pre-populated live regions, deviating from spec intent. role=alert is the spec's exception because the user agent SHOULD fire a system alert event on creation — but results are still inconsistent. Also flags a Firefox bug where aria-atomic="true" suppresses announcement entirely.

results.title: Screen reader support for ARIA live regions — TPGi
results.snippet: TPGi's longitudinal test-case writeup for topic (4), useful as the vendor-lab baseline against which later results are read. Establishes that live region support is browser-pair-dependent, not screen-reader-dependent: NVDA honored aria-live in Firefox but not IE; VoiceOver on iOS Safari only fired for assertive regions where macOS Safari handled both. Gives the concrete interference case relevant to design-time choice — adding aria-live to an error container causes double-speak in NVDA and JAWS and stops VoiceOver from honoring aria-describedby, i.e. the live region and the field description fight each other. Companion piece https://www.tpgi.com/aria-alert-support/ covers role=alert specifically.

results.title: ARIA and Assistive Technologies (ARIA-AT) — W3C Community Group project home
results.snippet: The project itself: a manual test suite whose tests are written as assertions of expected screen reader behavior against the APG's own design-pattern examples, run across desktop screen reader + browser combinations and reported back to AT vendors. This is the mechanism behind the support percentages, and the reason pattern choice is an interoperability bet — an APG example is not "supported" in the abstract, it is supported at a measured rate per AT. Published results live in the ARIA-AT App at https://aria-at.w3.org/reports (a JS app, so it must be opened in a browser rather than fetched as text).

results.title: Answering "What ARIA can I use?" — W3C Blog
results.snippet: W3C's own framing of why bad/unsupported ARIA is a real harm and not a style violation — directly supports topic (2). States the ARIA-AT objective in WCAG terms: to build consensus for definitions of "accessibility supported" / "actually works", because authors historically "get your site working with one AT and it ends up not working as well with another". Also supplies the honest coverage caveat that keeps this from being a compliance checkbox: at announcement only four UI patterns had support tables, with the goal scaled back to 30 examples across three desktop screen readers — so for most APG patterns, including several in the disclosure/menu/treegrid families, there is still no published interoperability data at all, and the design-time default should be the native element.

results.title: WebAIM: The WebAIM Million — 2026 report on the accessibility of the top 1,000,000 home pages
results.snippet: The primary source for the empirical harm claim the question asks to verify. Verbatim from the February 2026 report: "Home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (59.1 on average) than pages without ARIA (42 on average)." Also: "133,589,803 ARIA attributes were detected—over 133 per page on average! ARIA code increased 27% in just one year and is over 6 times higher than it was in 2019," and 82.7% of home pages used ARIA (excluding landmark roles), up from 79.4% in 2025. Critically, it carries its own causation caveat, which any honest citation must include: "Increased ARIA usage on pages was associated with higher detected errors. The more ARIA attributes that were present, the more detected accessibility errors could be expected. This does not necessarily mean that ARIA introduced these errors (these pages were also more complex), but pages typically had significantly more errors when more ARIA was present." Use this as correlation with a stated confound, not proof of causation.

results.title: Read Me First — ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) | W3C WAI
results.snippet: The canonical W3C home of "No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA," and the best design-time framing available. Two principles: (1) "A role is a promise" — declaring role="button" on a div commits you to the full keyboard model, and "Using a role without fulfilling the promise of that role is similar to making a 'Place Order' button that abandons an order and empties the shopping cart"; (2) ARIA "can cloak and enhance" — overriding native semantics silently deletes them, with named wrong cases: <table role="log"> (AT users no longer perceive a table) and <ul role="navigation"> (list structure destroyed). Stated harm: "Incorrect ARIA misrepresents visual experiences, with potentially devastating effects on their corresponding non-visual experiences" — for screen reader users "ARIA controls the rendering of their non-visual experience." This is the page that ties the contrarian rule to the APG pattern choices in topic (1).

results.title: Using ARIA — W3C (Discontinued Draft, 24 February 2026)
results.snippet:
The primary source for the "rules of ARIA use" — note for accuracy that the current document states four rules, not five, and is explicitly a Discontinued Draft: "the four rules of ARIA are kept for historical purposes and for easier reference, but there are no plans to continue work on this document," pointing readers to the APG instead. Rule 1: "If you can use a native HTML element ... with the semantics and behavior you require already built in, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible, then do so." Rule 2: "Do not change native semantics, unless you really have to" — with the concrete wrong/right pair

vs

heading tab

. Rule 3: all interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard usable. Rule 4: do not use role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element. Cite the count as four (with the historical fifth, accessible names, now folded elsewhere) rather than repeating the common "five rules" blog phrasing.

results.title: ARIA in HTML — W3C Recommendation, 15 April 2026
results.snippet: The normative, machine-checkable version of "ARIA is the wrong answer here" — the only source in this set with MUST NOT force. Authors "MUST NOT use the ARIA role and aria-* attributes in a manner that conflicts with the semantics" in its conformance tables. Named prohibitions useful as design-time guardrails: no role or aria-* on base/head/meta/link, input type=hidden, col, colgroup, map, noscript, script, slot, source, style, template; aria-hidden="true" must not go on <body>; aria-checked must not be used on input type=checkbox/radio (the native state is authoritative); datalist takes no aria-*; img with no accessible name is limited to none/presentation; label associated with a labelable element cannot have its role changed. Also directs conformance checkers to flag redundant roles, deprecated roles, and abstract roles. Being a REC, this is what you cite when a team argues a role override is "just a preference."

results.title: WebAIM: Introduction to ARIA — Accessible Rich Internet Applications
results.snippet:
WebAIM's own prose companion to the Million data, and the best short list of concrete cases where ARIA is wrong and native HTML or a layout change is right. "ARIA should not be used when HTML provides sufficient semantics for accessibility! When used incorrectly, ARIA can introduce significant accessibility barriers." Named failures with described harm: role="navigation" on a
    destroys list semantics (screen readers stop announcing item counts and list navigation) — correct fix is a wrapper,
      …
    , i.e. a markup/layout change rather than a role; role="button" on a div makes AT announce a button that keyboard users cannot activate; aria-label overrides visible

results.title: ARIA Spec for the Uninitiated: Part 1 — Deque
results.snippet: Deque technical writeup useful only where W3C prose is thin: it explains why an ARIA role rewrites the accessibility tree node rather than layering onto it, which is the mechanism behind the APG "cloak" warning and behind the WebAIM cases (role on <ul> replacing the list node, aria-label replacing rather than supplementing the accessible name computation). Secondary to the four W3C/WebAIM sources above — use it for the accessibility-tree explanation, not for any of the rules or numbers, which should be cited from source.

claims.claim: In moderated user testing of five SPA route-change prototypes with assistive technology users (NVDA+Chrome, JAWS+Firefox, ZoomText, Dragon NaturallySpeaking, switch access), moving focus to a heading element inside the newly rendered content was the best-performing technique for screen reader users.
claims.quote: Focusing on a heading was found to be the best experience, as it would save time and make it clear what happened.

claims.claim: Resetting focus to the top of the app or to the application wrapper on route change was rejected by testers as harmful, not merely suboptimal — the common 'focus the app container' pattern fails in large applications.
claims.quote: resetting focus to the top of the app would be very overwhelming, especially in large applications

claims.claim: The recommended pattern that emerged is not a single focus target but a hybrid: an opt-in skip-link component that receives focus on route change, paired with an ARIA live region announcing the current page name, with developer control over DOM position and label.
claims.quote: The most accessible and best performing pattern will likely be an opt-in component where the developer can specify where the control should go in the DOM and how it should be labeled.

claims.claim: Having a <main> landmark in the markup does not make the main region keyboard-reachable — keyboard-only testers could not reach main in the prototypes despite the landmark being present, meaning a focusable target (skip link or tabindex=-1 element) is required in addition to the landmark.
claims.quote: couldn't get to the main region in the prototypes with the keyboard alone

claims.claim: Focusing a wrapper element around new content, and NVDA's handling of <main>, produced measurable degradation: wrapper focus was too subtle to be noticed, and NVDA duplicated content and emitted extra announcements around the main element — a cross-screen-reader inconsistency in route-change focus handling.
claims.quote: In NVDA, there was some duplicate reading of content and `<main>` was doing some extra announcements–seemed like a screen reader quirk.

claims.claim: MDN names focus confusion and abnormal live-region announcement behavior as concrete accessibility failure modes caused by old and new content being simultaneously present in the DOM during an SPA view change — directly linking the SPA transition problem (research topic 3) to the live-region problem (topic 4).
claims.quote: Accessibility issues like loss of reading position, focus confusion, and strange live region announcement behavior can also result from having the new and old content both present in the DOM at once.

claims.claim: The View Transition API exposes Document.startViewTransition() as the entry point for same-document (SPA) transitions, returning a ViewTransition object representing the in-flight transition — the object a developer must hook to sequence focus moves against DOM replacement.
claims.quote: Starts a new same-document (SPA) view transition and returns a `ViewTransition` object to represent it.

claims.claim: The API includes built-in facilities for skipping the transition animation under developer-specified circumstances, which is the documented hook for honoring prefers-reduced-motion rather than a workaround.
claims.quote: there are features that allow you to both customize the transition animation and manipulate the view transition itself (for example specify circumstances under which the animation is skipped), for both SPA and MPA view transitions

claims.claim: Cross-document (MPA) view transitions are opt-in via the @view-transition at-rule declared in BOTH the current and destination documents, with PageRevealEvent and PageSwapEvent providing script access to the ViewTransition object from the navigated-to and navigated-from documents respectively.
claims.quote: In the case of a cross-document navigation, `@view-transition` is used to opt in the current and destination documents to undergo a view transition.

claims.claim: This MDN overview page acknowledges the accessibility hazards of view transitions but supplies no remediation guidance — no focus-management pattern, no prefers-reduced-motion handling, and no aria-live guidance — deferring all of it to separate 'Using' guides; it is therefore not a usable authority for correct focus behavior on route change.
claims.quote: For more information, see: [Using the View Transition API](/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using) * [Using view transition types](/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using_types) * [Using element-scoped view transitions](/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using_element-scoped)

claims.claim: For prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, the author recommends setting an extremely short animation duration (animation-duration: 0.001s !important) on the ::view-transition-old(*) and ::view-transition-new(*) pseudo-elements rather than animation: none, because a zero/none duration suppresses the animationend event that JavaScript listeners may be bound to.
claims.quote: An important note here, setting a duration protects functionality involving eventlisteners bound to the `animationEnd` event.

claims.claim: Reduced-motion handling for the View Transitions API must be applied to the API's own generated pseudo-elements (::view-transition-old / ::view-transition-new), not only to author-written CSS animations and transitions — i.e. an existing site-wide prefers-reduced-motion block does not automatically cover view transitions.
claims.quote: Equally as important and future-proofing, we can also set View Transitions API 'old' and 'new' state animation duration.

claims.claim: The motivating population figure the author cites for reduced-motion support is that roughly 35% of adults over 40 experience balance dysfunction, attributed to a National Library of Medicine study.
claims.quote: around 35% of adults over 40 years old experience balance dysfunction

claims.claim: Vestibular disorders are framed as affecting both balance and visual perception, which is the stated mechanism by which page/view transition animation causes harm.
claims.quote: People with vestibular disorders have a problem with their inner ear. It affects their balance as well as their visual perception of their world around them.

claims.claim: Deque's stated prescription for SPA route/view changes is that the change must be made perceivable to screen reader users by one or more of three mechanisms — page title announcement, ARIA live regions, or focus management — presented as alternatives rather than a single mandated behavior; the post specifies no focus destination, no skip-link role, and does not mention focus being lost to document body.
claims.quote: Make sure that client-side view changes are known to screen reader users by announcing the change in page title, using ARIA live regions and/or focus management.

claims.claim: Accessibility is framed as cheaper and easier when handled at the UX/design stage rather than as a later code fix — a direct practitioner statement of the design-time-decision thesis, from Deque (axe-core's maintainer).
claims.quote: It's easier and less costly to incorporate accessibility the earlier you tackle it, starting with UX and Design.

claims.claim: The ARIA Authoring Practices Guide is positioned as the reference to consult for known interaction patterns when prototyping complex or custom interactions, and that prototyping should happen early — i.e. pattern selection is treated as a design-phase step, not an implementation detail.
claims.quote: Prototype complex or custom interactions early, and include accessibility. Check out the ARIA Authoring Practices for known interaction patterns.

claims.claim: Semantic HTML structure is asserted to take priority over developer ergonomics regardless of CSS/JS tooling — the native-element-first position that underlies the 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' rule, though the post never states that rule or the five rules of ARIA use.
claims.quote: Semantic structure is more important than developer ergonomics. Craft the most semantic HTML pages you can, regardless of your CSS or JavaScript development tools.

claims.claim: Making every element focusable is explicitly identified as unnecessary because screen readers provide navigation modes other than the TAB key — a falsifiable constraint on how designers should scope the tab order in SPA views.
claims.quote: Screen readers have ways of navigating other than using the TAB key, so you don't need to make everything focusable.

claims.claim: The practitioner consensus in this thread is that on SPA route change focus should move to a non-landmark, non-interactive element (typically the page's H1 heading) rather than to a landmark element such as <main> or <footer>, or to a link or button.
claims.quote: "Your focus element should not be a landmark (main, footer etc.)" ... the original author implemented focusing on the first H1 element combined with an aria-live region for announcements: "focus on a heading element seemed OK"

claims.claim: Focusing a container div on route change causes screen readers to read out the entire contents of the container, producing a confusing announcement — so the focus target must be a specific small element, not a wrapper.
claims.quote: "If you set your element to a container div, it will read the contents. (Confusing to users)"

claims.claim: The focus target must carry tabindex="-1" to be programmatically focusable, and this attribute has a documented side effect: it changes the natural tab order behavior after a click, so Tab no longer moves to the next focusable element near the click point.
claims.quote: "You need to give your focus element a tabindex of -1. (To allow focus)" ... "It disrupts the expected accessibility behavior, where clicking on the page and subsequently pressing the 'Tab' key should naturally focus on the next focussable element within the vicinity of the click."

claims.claim: Marcy Sutton's recommendation, cited in this thread, is a two-part pattern: a labelled skip link that receives focus on route change plus an ARIA live region present on page load to which the new page name is appended after navigation — and that focus should be set only when the user initiated the navigation by activating a link.
claims.quote: "Provide a skip link that takes focus on a route change within the site, with a label that indicates what the link will do when activated" ... "Include an ARIA Live Region on page load. On a route change, append text to it indicating the current page" ... "Setting focus when the user initiates the action by activating a link is a better approach"

claims.claim: React Router shipped no built-in route-change focus management for years; the maintainer explicitly declined to make a recommendation, leaving the behavior (focus lost to document body on route change) as the framework default.
claims.quote: Michael Jackson (React Router maintainer) acknowledged the importance but expressed caution: "I've been hesitant to make recommendations since I don't want to cause more harm than good."

result.publishDate: 2017-06-05 (original post; later converted to Discussion #9863 in the remix-run/react-router repo; 36 comments and 2 replies; marked superseded by issue #9555)

claims.claim: Client-side rendering frameworks (React, Vue, Ember, Angular) break the browser's default post-navigation focus and announcement behavior, making focus management and screen reader announcement an explicit developer/design obligation rather than something the platform handles.
claims.quote: When building JavaScript-heavy websites and web applications with popular frameworks and libraries like React, Vue, Ember, Angular and so on, parts of a page can change without a traditional page reload (we call them "view changes"). This paradigm requires developers to manually manage focus and screen reader announcements to ensure assistive technology and keyboard-only users aren't left behind while sighted mouse users can follow along.

claims.claim: As of March 2019 there was no settled best practice in the accessibility community for SPA route-change focus: the competing candidates were sending focus to a heading, sending focus to a wrapper element, and announcing the change via an ARIA live region — and experts disagreed on which is correct.
claims.quote: Except those of us in the community who work with accessibility regularly still can't quite agree on a best practice: should we send focus to a heading, or a wrapper element? Should we announce a page change with ARIA live regions?

claims.claim: The variable actually under test across the routing prototypes is exactly two things: the DOM location keyboard focus lands on after the view swap, and what (if anything) the screen reader announces — i.e. the route-change decision reduces to focus destination plus announcement.
claims.quote: The differences lie in how keyboard focus is handled with JavaScript: where it leaves a keyboard or screen reader user on the page, and what information (if any) is announced in the screen reader.

claims.claim: This post is a recruitment/methodology announcement, not a results report; the empirical findings from testing these routing prototypes with disabled users were produced in July 2019 with Fable Tech Labs and published on the Gatsby blog, which is where the actual comparative data lives.
claims.quote: Update: In July 2019, I worked with Fable Tech Labs to conduct research on client-side routing and accessibility using the prototypes outlined in this post. You can read the results on the Gatsby blog: https://www.gatsbyjs.org/blog/2019-07-11-user-testing-accessible-client-routing/

claims.claim: Even a router explicitly designed for accessibility (Reach Router for React) did not resolve which route-change focus technique is correct, indicating the problem is a design-level decision rather than one solvable by library defaults alone.
claims.quote: Even with tools like Reach Router for React, which was developed with accessibility in mind, there are still questions about which technique works best.

claims.claim: The APG treats Grid and Table as two distinct patterns separated by interactivity, not by visual appearance: a table is explicitly defined as non-interactive, while a grid is defined by directional-key navigation — so choosing 'grid' commits the design to a keyboard navigation model, and Treegrid adds hierarchy plus editable/interactive cells on top of that.
claims.quote: Grid: "A container that enables users to navigate information or interactive elements using directional navigation keys." / Table: "A static tabular structure containing rows and cells; it is not an interactive widget." / Treegrid: "A hierarchical data grid consisting of tabular information that is editable or interactive."

claims.claim: Disclosure, Accordion, and Tabs are three separate APG patterns with distinct structural definitions — disclosure is a single expand/collapse toggle, accordion is a vertically stacked set of interactive headings over sections, tabs is a set of layered panels showing exactly one at a time — meaning the choice among them is a layout/content-structure decision made before any code.
claims.quote: Disclosure: "A widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible)." / Accordion: "A vertically stacked set of interactive headings that each contain a title, content snippet, or thumbnail representing a section of content." / Tabs: "A set of layered sections of content, known as tab panels, that display one panel of content at a time."

claims.claim: The APG separates Alert from Alert Dialog on the axis of interruption and required response: an alert delivers a message without interrupting the user's task, whereas an alert dialog is a modal that interrupts the workflow and acquires a response — an interaction-design decision, not a markup detail.
claims.quote: Alert: "An element that displays a brief, important message without interrupting the user's task." / Alert and Message Dialogs: "An alert dialog is a modal dialog that interrupts the user's workflow to communicate an important message and acquire a response." / Dialog (Modal): "A window overlaid on either the primary window or another dialog window."

claims.claim: Combobox and Listbox are distinguished in the APG by the presence of a text input with an associated popup versus a plain selectable option list; Menu/Menubar is defined as a list of actions or functions while Toolbar is defined as a container grouping controls — so the popup and the action-versus-selection distinction, not the visual styling, determines the pattern.
claims.quote: Combobox: "An input widget that has an associated popup." / Listbox: "A widget that presents a list of options and allows a user to select one or more of them." / Menu and Menubar: "A widget that offers a list of choices to the user, such as a set of actions or functions." / Toolbar: "A container for grouping a set of controls, such as buttons, menubuttons, or checkboxes."

claims.claim: The APG patterns index enumerates a fixed, closed catalog of 30 named patterns (Accordion, Alert, Alert and Message Dialogs, Breadcrumb, Button, Carousel, Checkbox, Combobox, Dialog (Modal), Disclosure, Feed, Grid, Landmarks, Link, Listbox, Menu and Menubar, Menu Button, Meter, Radio Group, Slider, Slider (Multi-Thumb), Spinbutton, Switch, Table, Tabs, Toolbar, Tooltip, Tree View, Treegrid, Window Splitter), framed as guidance for building accessibility semantics into widgets rather than as a code library.
claims.quote: "How to build accessibility semantics into web patterns and widgets"

claims.claim: The APG constrains a combobox's popup to exactly four roles — listbox, tree, grid, or dialog — so the designer's choice of what the popup *is* (a flat list vs. a hierarchy vs. a tabular result set vs. a full dialog) is itself the ARIA decision, and it further dictates aria-haspopup: the attribute is required only when the popup is something other than a listbox.
claims.quote: The popup is an element that has role `listbox`, `tree`, `grid`, or `dialog`. ... If the popup has a role other than `listbox`, the element with role `combobox` has `aria-haspopup` set to a value that corresponds to the popup type.

claims.claim: Choosing the combobox pattern commits the implementation to a virtual-focus model: DOM focus must remain on the combobox input while assistive-technology focus moves through the popup via aria-activedescendant — with dialog popups as the single documented exception, where real DOM focus does move into the popup.
claims.quote: When a descendant of a listbox, grid, or tree popup is focused, DOM focus remains on the combobox and the combobox has `aria-activedescendant` set to a value that refers to the focused element within the popup. ... Unlike other combobox popups, dialogs do not support `aria-activedescendant` so DOM focus moves into the dialog from the combobox.

claims.claim: The pattern obliges a specific, non-obvious tab-order design: the popup, everything inside it, and the popup's trigger icon/button are all removed from the page Tab sequence — meaning a designer cannot spec 'Tab into the dropdown' or a separately tabbable chevron button without breaking the pattern.
claims.quote: Note: The popup indicator icon or button (if present), the popup, and the popup descendants are excluded from the page Tab sequence.

claims.claim: The APG formally names the editable vs. select-only distinction as the fork that separates combobox from listbox and menu button: a combobox's differentiating feature is that the chosen value appears in an editable field the user can select and copy, which is a visual/interaction decision made at design time, not a coding detail.
claims.quote: If a combobox does not support text input, it is referred to as select-only, meaning the only way users can set its value is by selecting a value in the popup. ... One feature that distinguishes combobox from both listbox and menu button is that the user's choice can be presented as a value in an editable field, which gives users the ability to select some or all of the value for copying to the clipboard.

claims.claim: The APG defines four named autocomplete behaviors (none; list with manual selection; list with automatic selection; list with inline autocomplete) that map onto aria-autocomplete values none/list/both, so picking 'does the first suggestion auto-highlight?' or 'does a completion string appear inline after the cursor?' is a design-time spec decision that determines the required ARIA value and the visible state.
claims.quote: List with inline autocomplete: This is the same as list with automatic selection with one additional feature. The portion of the selected suggestion that has not been typed by the user, a completion string, appears inline after the input cursor in the combobox.

claims.claim: The APG defines the grid-vs-table choice by tab-sequence behavior, not by markup: a grid is a composite widget in which exactly one focusable element is in the page tab sequence, whereas in a table every focusable element it contains is in the tab sequence. This makes 'grid or table?' a keyboard-model decision that must be settled at design time, since it determines how many tab stops the component costs.
claims.quote: A `grid` is a composite widget so it: Always contains multiple focusable elements. Only one of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence. ... All focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence.

claims.claim: Choosing the grid pattern obliges the author to implement focus management inside the widget — the browser's native tab order no longer does the work. Grid is therefore not a styling or markup choice but a commitment to build and maintain a roving-focus implementation.
claims.quote: Requires the author to provide code that manages focus movement inside it.

claims.claim: The grid pattern commits the component to a specific, non-negotiable arrow-key model with defined edge behavior: Right Arrow moves one cell right and focus does not move at the row's right-most cell; Home moves to the first cell in the focused row; Control+Home moves to the first cell of the first row. These are interaction commitments a designer inherits the moment the pattern is picked.
claims.quote: Right Arrow: Moves focus one cell to the right. If focus is on the right-most cell in the row, focus does not move. ... Home: moves focus to the first cell in the row that contains focus. ... Control + Home: moves focus to the first cell in the first row.

claims.claim: The APG sanctions grid for two distinct purposes — data grids (tabular information) and layout grids (grouping other widgets) — and justifies the layout-grid use explicitly as a way to cut the number of tab stops on a page. This is a layout/information-architecture decision made in design, not a remediation applied to shipped code.
claims.quote: Uses of the `grid` pattern broadly fall into two categories: presenting tabular information (data grids) and grouping other widgets (layout grids). ... Since only one element in the entire grid is included in the tab sequence, grouping with a grid can dramatically reduce the number of tab stops on a page.

claims.claim: The APG states that assistive-technology experience quality in a grid depends jointly on what each cell contains and where keyboard focus lands, and names the workable combinations: a cell holding one widget that does not itself need arrow keys (focus set on that widget), or a cell holding text or a single graphic (focus set on the cell). Deciding cell contents therefore decides the focus model.
claims.quote: For assistive technology users, the quality of experience when navigating a grid heavily depends on both what a cell contains and on where keyboard focus is set. ... A cell contains one widget whose operation does not require arrow keys and grid navigation keys set focus on that widget...A cell contains text or a single graphic and grid navigation keys set focus on the cell.

claims.claim: The APG defines the menu/menubar choice as a visual-persistence decision, not a code decision: a menubar IS a menu that is permanently visible (typically horizontal, desktop-application-style), so choosing 'menubar' commits the design to an always-rendered persistent bar while choosing 'menu' commits it to a transient popup opened by a menu button, a parent item, or a context command.
claims.quote: A menu is usually opened, or made visible, by activating a menu button, choosing an item in a menu that opens a sub menu, or by invoking a command, such as Shift + F10 in Windows, that opens a context specific menu. When a user activates a choice in a menu, the menu usually closes unless the choice opened a submenu. A menu that is visually persistent is a menubar. A menubar is typically horizontal and is often used to create a menu bar similar to those found near the top of the window in many desktop applications, offering the user quick access to a consistent set of commands.

claims.claim: Adopting the menu/menubar pattern obliges a composite-widget keyboard model in which Tab is removed as the intra-widget navigation key: Tab/Shift+Tab move focus into or entirely out of the widget (closing all menus), and arrow keys become the only way to move between items — implemented either via roving tabindex (all items tabindex=-1, first menubar item tabindex=0) or aria-activedescendant.
claims.quote: Because menubar and menu elements are composite widgets as described in the practice for Keyboard Navigation Inside Components, Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus among the items in the menu. Instead, the keyboard commands described in this section enable users to move focus among the elements in a menubar or menu. […] When focus is on a menuitem in a menu or menubar, move focus out of the menu or menubar, and close all menus and submenus. […] Each item in the menu has tabindex set to -1, except in a menubar, where the first item has tabindex set to 0.

claims.claim: The pattern mandates specific focus-management behavior that the design must accommodate: opening a menu (or focusing a menubar) must place keyboard focus on the first item, and Escape must both close the menu containing focus and return focus to the element that opened it — with authors explicitly responsible for moving focus into a non-persistent menu on open.
claims.quote: When a menu opens, or when a menubar receives focus, keyboard focus is placed on the first item. […] Unlike a menubar, a menu is not visually persistent, and authors are responsible for ensuring focus moves to an item inside of a menu when the menu opens. […] Escape: Close the menu that contains focus and return focus to the element or context, e.g., menu button or parent menuitem, from which the menu was opened.

claims.claim: The pattern requires machine-readable state that must mirror what is visually shown: a parent menuitem must carry aria-haspopup and must flip aria-expanded to true exactly when its child menu is visible, and menuitemcheckbox/menuitemradio must set aria-checked=true when checked — so any visual open/closed or checked affordance in the design has a mandatory ARIA counterpart.
claims.quote: A parent menuitem has aria-haspopup set to either menu or true. A parent menuitem has aria-expanded set to false when its child menu is not visible and set to true when the child menu is visible. […] When a menuitemcheckbox or menuitemradio is checked, aria-checked is set to true.

claims.claim: Layout orientation is an ARIA-bearing design decision: menubar defaults to horizontal and menu defaults to vertical, so a designer who lays a menubar out vertically (or a menu horizontally) obliges an explicit aria-orientation override, and the arrow-key mappings invert accordingly (Down behaves as Right and vice versa).
claims.quote: If a menubar is vertically oriented, it has aria-orientation set to vertical. The default value of aria-orientation for a menubar is horizontal. […] If a menu is horizontally oriented, it has aria-orientation set to horizontal. The default value of aria-orientation for a menu is vertical. […] When items in a menubar are arranged vertically and items in menu containers are arranged horizontally: Down Arrow performs as Right Arrow is described above, and vice versa.

claims.claim: The APG disclosure pattern commits the designer to a two-key-only keyboard model — Enter and Space toggle visibility, with no arrow-key navigation, roving tabindex, or Home/End keys — which is what distinguishes it operationally from the tabs and accordion patterns.
claims.quote: Enter: activates the disclosure control and toggles the visibility of the disclosure content. Space: activates the disclosure control and toggles the visibility of the disclosure content.

claims.claim: Choosing disclosure obliges a programmatically exposed expanded/collapsed state: the control must carry role button with aria-expanded set to true when content is visible and false when hidden.
claims.quote: The element that shows and hides the content has role button. When the content is visible, the element with role `button` has aria-expanded set to `true`. When the content area is hidden, it is set to `false`.

claims.claim: The disclosure pattern is structurally exactly two elements — one trigger button and one controlled content region — so it carries no grouping, no set-position semantics, and no single-open/multi-open policy, unlike accordion or tabs.
claims.quote: A disclosure is a widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible). It has two elements: a disclosure button and a section of content whose visibility is controlled by the button.

claims.claim: aria-controls is optional in the disclosure pattern, not required — the association between button and content is not a mandated part of the contract, contrary to common assumption.
claims.quote: Optionally, the element with role `button` has a value specified for aria-controls that refers to the element that contains all the content that is shown or hidden.

claims.claim: The APG specifies a visual affordance commitment for disclosure at design time: a push-button appearance with a right-pointing arrow/triangle when collapsed that rotates to point down when expanded, making the state visible sighted-side as well as in the accessibility tree.
claims.quote: When the controlled content is hidden, the button is often styled as a typical push button with a right-pointing arrow or triangle to hint that activating the button will display additional content. When the content is visible, the arrow or triangle typically points down.

claims.claim: The APG obliges any element marked role=dialog with aria-modal=true to contain its tab sequence: Tab and Shift+Tab cycle within the dialog and never move focus outside it, and Escape must close it. Choosing the modal dialog pattern therefore commits the design to a closed keyboard loop plus a keyboard dismissal affordance.
claims.quote: Like non-modal dialogs, modal dialogs contain their tab sequence…However, unlike most non-modal dialogs, modal dialogs do not provide means for moving keyboard focus outside the dialog window without closing the dialog. […] Tab: Moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog. If focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first tabbable element inside the dialog. […] Escape: Closes the dialog.

claims.claim: The APG specifies mandatory focus movement at both boundaries of a dialog's lifecycle: on open, focus moves into the dialog; on close, focus returns to the invoking element (with narrow stated exceptions). This is the same open/close focus contract that route-change focus management in SPAs is modeled on, and it rules out leaving focus on document body.
claims.quote: When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog. […] When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless either: The invoking element no longer exists…[or] The work flow design includes [specific conditions]. […] Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog.

claims.claim: aria-modal=true is conditioned on a VISUAL design commitment, not only a code one: the APG permits marking a dialog modal only when application code blocks all interaction outside it AND visual styling obscures the outside content. The ARIA attribute is thus a design-time decision that the visual layer must honor.
claims.quote: Mark a dialog modal only when both: Application code prevents all users from interacting in any way with content outside of it. Visual styling obscures the content outside of it. […] Inert content outside an active dialog is typically visually obscured or dimmed so it is difficult to discern.

claims.claim: The APG names a specific bad-ARIA harm: aria-modal=true applied to a dialog that does not actually behave modally hides outside content from some assistive technology users, producing what W3C calls 'severe negative ramifications' — a concrete case where adding an ARIA attribute is worse than omitting it.
claims.quote: Because marking a dialog modal by setting aria-modal to true can prevent users of some assistive technologies from perceiving content outside the dialog, users of those technologies will experience severe negative ramifications if a dialog is marked modal but does not behave as a modal for other users.

claims.claim: Where initial focus lands inside a dialog is a content-design decision, not a default: the APG prescribes different targets depending on content structure and consequence — a static element with tabindex="-1" for semantically rich or long content, and the least destructive action for irreversible operations.
claims.quote: If the dialog content includes semantic structures, such as lists, tables, or multiple paragraphs, that need to be perceived in order to easily understand the content... then it is advisable to add tabindex="-1" to a static element at the start of the content and initially focus that element. […] If a dialog contains the final step in a process that is not easily reversible, such as deleting data or completing a financial transaction, it may be advisable to set focus on the least destructive action.
