claims.claim: W3C requires the live region container to already exist in the DOM at page load — injecting a new element that itself carries role=alert/aria-live will not be announced by most screen readers; the technique's own test procedure fails a page whose error container is created at error time.
claims.quote: The error container must be present in the DOM on page load for the error message to be spoken by most screen readers.

claims.claim: role=alert is defined by W3C as functionally equivalent to aria-live="assertive", so using both on the same element is redundant rather than additive.
claims.quote: equivalent to using `aria-live=assertive`

claims.claim: aria-atomic="true" is required on the alert container specifically to make VoiceOver on iOS re-announce error text on a second and subsequent invalid submission — a documented, screen-reader-specific failure mode, not a general-purpose best practice.
claims.quote: is necessary to make Voiceover on iOS read the error messages after more than one invalid submission

claims.claim: W3C's own reference implementation inserts an artificial ~500ms delay between clearing the live region and injecting the new error text, indicating that immediate same-tick DOM replacement is unreliable for announcement.
claims.quote: Wait 500 milliseconds, then show the errors

claims.claim: The conformance test for this technique is structural and checkable at design/markup review time: an empty container with role=alert or aria-live=assertive present at load, plus injection into that already-present container — steps 1 and 3 must both be true.
claims.quote: 1. Determine that an empty error container with `role=alert` or `aria-live=assertive` attribute is present in the DOM at page load. 2. Trigger the error that causes the content in the live region to appear or update. 3. Determine that the error message was injected into the already present error container.

claims.claim: Screen reader support for aria-live is inconsistent across screen reader/browser pairs even for a trivial button-triggered text update: JAWS 15 announced the region in both Firefox 27 and IE 11, NVDA 2014.1 announced it in Firefox but not IE, Window Eyes 8.4 announced it in Firefox only when aria-live was assertive and never in IE, and VoiceOver on iOS Safari 7.0 announced it only when the region was assertive (VoiceOver on OS X Safari 7.0.2 worked fully). This is the documented cross-screen-reader failure mode, though the data is from March 2014 and covers browsers/AT versions now obsolete.
claims.quote: For the common use case of triggering a live region update based on activation of a standard control, Jaws 15 fully supports the ARIA live region in both Firefox 27 and Internet Explorer 11. NVDA 2014.1 supports the aria-live attribute in Firefox, but not Internet Explorer. Window Eyes 8.4 only supports the ARIA live region in Firefox when the aria-live attribute is set to assertive. It doesn’t support it in Internet Explorer. VoiceOver in Safari 7.0.2 (OSX) fully supports the ARIA live region, but in Safari 7.0 (iOS) the test case only worked when the live region was assertive.

claims.claim: Adding role="status" on top of aria-live="polite" changed announcement behavior for some screen reader/browser combinations and not others — it made Window Eyes recognise the polite live region in Firefox, but made no difference to VoiceOver in Safari on iOS, or to Window Eyes or NVDA in Internet Explorer. So role=status is not a universal fix for a live region that fails to announce.
claims.quote: From the screen reader point of view, adding the status role forces Window Eyes to recognise the polite ARIA live region in Firefox. However it doesn’t make any difference to VoiceOver in Safari (iOS), or Window Eyes or NVDA in Internet Explorer.

claims.claim: The combination best supported across the tested matrix was aria-live="assertive" together with role="status", leaving only NVDA and Window Eyes in Internet Explorer unsupportive — but the author explicitly warns against reaching for assertive by default because it interrupts the screen reader's current task, and warns that behavior degrades in real-world complexity beyond these minimal test cases.
claims.quote: With these simple test cases, the most widely supported combination is to use aria-live=”assertive” with role=”status” to create the ARIA live region. […] An assertive ARIA live region isn’t always desireable. Remember the notification will interrupt the screen reader from its current task, so use aria-live=”assertive” with care. The test cases used here are extraordinarily simple. When ARIA live regions are used in the wild (in more complex scenarios), screen reader behaviour is known to become more erratic.

claims.claim: aria-live takes exactly three values with distinct interruption semantics — off (no notification), polite (screen reader notifies once the current task is complete), and assertive (screen reader interrupts the current task) — which makes polite vs assertive a decision about whether the update is worth interrupting the user, not a coding detail.
claims.quote: The aria-live attribute identifies an element as a live region. It takes three possible values: Off (no notification). Polite (screen reader notifies user once current task is complete). Assertive (screen reader interrupts current task to notify user).

claims.claim: role="status" is defined as advisory information the user should be made aware of but which is not important enough to warrant an alert, and because it is itself a live region an element with role=status should not receive focus — i.e. status announces without moving focus, distinguishing it from alert and from focus-moving patterns.
claims.quote: The status role indicates that the element contains advisory information that the user should be made aware of, but which isn’t important enough to warrant an alert. The status role is a form of live region, so an element with the status role applied should not receive focus.

claims.claim: In the 2026 WebAIM Million, home pages that used ARIA averaged 59.1 detected accessibility errors versus 42 on pages with no ARIA — roughly 17 more detected barriers per page — which is the headline empirical support for the 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' rule.
claims.quote: Home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (59.1 on average) than pages without ARIA (42 on average).

claims.claim: WebAIM explicitly disclaims causation for the ARIA/error correlation, attributing part of the gap to page complexity — so the statistic is correlational evidence, not proof that ARIA itself introduces the errors.
claims.quote: This does not necessarily mean that ARIA introduced these errors (these pages were also more complex).

claims.claim: The correlation is dose-dependent: the more ARIA attributes present on a page, the more detected accessibility errors were expected.
claims.quote: Increased ARIA usage on pages was associated with higher detected errors. The more ARIA attributes that were present, the more detected accessibility errors could be expected.

claims.claim: The ARIA menu pattern specifically is measurably mis-implemented in the wild: 5.7% of the top million home pages used role="menu", and 22% of those menus actively introduced accessibility barriers because the required menu markup and keyboard interactions were absent.
claims.quote: 5.7% of home pages had an ARIA menu (`role="menu"`), but 22% of those ARIA menus introduced accessibility barriers due to the lack of necessary ARIA menu markup and interactions.

claims.claim: ARIA volume is large and growing — 133,589,803 ARIA attributes across the sample (over 133 per page on average), up 27% year over year and over 6x 2019 levels, with 82.7% of pages using ARIA (excluding landmark roles); aria-hidden="true" alone averaged 23.3 per page, up 30% from 2025.
claims.quote: 133,589,803 ARIA attributes were detected—over 133 per page on average!

claims.claim: JAWS does not honor the polite/assertive distinction at all: in current testing (JAWS 2026.2512.50 + Chrome 143/144), every live region type — aria-live="polite", aria-live="assertive", role="alert", and <output> — is announced as polite, so choosing assertive buys nothing for JAWS users.
claims.quote: All live regions treated as polite (announces at first break, which is not at end of sentence).

claims.claim: role="alert" does not reliably produce a spoken "alert" prefix: of seven screen reader/browser pairs tested, only NVDA/Firefox prepends the word "alert"; JAWS/Chrome, Narrator/Edge, VoiceOver macOS/Safari, TalkBack/Chrome, and VoiceOver iPadOS/Safari all omit it, so the role's semantic signal is lost for most users.
claims.quote: alert role does not pre-pend announcement with alert .

claims.claim: A live region hidden by any of hidden, aria-hidden, or display:none is never announced — this held across all seven screen reader/browser combinations tested and is the only row in the support matrix marked unambiguously "yes", confirming the region must be present and unhidden in the DOM at injection time.
claims.quote: No live region announces when hidden

claims.claim: VoiceOver on macOS (12.6.6/Safari 16.5 and 26.0.1/Safari 26.0.1, i.e. unfixed across four years) has a polite-region bug: aria-live="polite" and <output> are silently dropped during read-all, yet behave assertively on Braille displays and drop content there.
claims.quote: aria-live="polite" is not announced during read-all ( Ctrl + Opt + A ), but acts assertive in Braille displays and some content is lost.

claims.claim: Some screen readers drop specific live-region mechanisms entirely: Orca on Ubuntu 24.10 and 25.04 with Firefox never announces role="alert", and Narrator with Edge never announces the HTML <output> element even though Chrome and Firefox expose it as a status region.
claims.quote: alert role not announced at all.

claims.claim: Assistive technology normally conveys only *changes* to a live region, not its initial contents, so the spec requires authors to render an empty live region early (e.g. on page load) and inject content afterward; role=alert is the single named exception because system alert events fire when it is rendered.
claims.quote: Typically, assistive technology will only convey changes to a live region, not the initial contents of a live region. To ensure content in a live region is announced, authors SHOULD create a rendered but empty live region as early as possible (such as on page load), and then modify the content of the live region when the author expects changes to be spoken or brailled. The exception to this live region convention is alert , due to system accessibility notifications events required for the role. While an alert is a live region, its content is announced by assistive technology when the alert is rendered on the page and when the content changes.

claims.claim: role=alert and role=status are not stylistic synonyms: alert carries an implicit aria-live="assertive" plus aria-atomic="true", while status carries an implicit aria-live="polite" plus aria-atomic="true" — so choosing the role is choosing the interruption model. The spec also directs authors to use alertdialog instead of alert whenever focus is meant to move to the message, and to keep status from taking focus.
claims.quote: Elements with the role alert have an implicit aria-live value of assertive , and an implicit aria-atomic value of true . […] If an author desires focus to move to a message when it is conveyed, the author SHOULD use alertdialog instead of alert . […] Elements with the role status have an implicit aria-live value of polite and an implicit aria-atomic value of true . […] Authors SHOULD ensure an element with role status does not receive focus as a result of change in status.

claims.claim: The spec normatively discourages assertive: polite updates SHOULD be announced at the next graceful opportunity, assertive updates SHOULD be announced immediately and may clear the speech queue of previously queued changes, and authors SHOULD NOT use assertive unless the interruption is imperative — with the stated harm being that interruption can disorient users or cause them not to complete their current task.
claims.quote: When live regions are marked as polite , assistive technologies SHOULD announce updates at the next graceful opportunity, such as at the end of speaking the current sentence or when the user pauses typing. When live regions are marked as assertive , assistive technologies SHOULD immediately notify the user of modifications to the live region. Because an interruption might disorient users or cause them to not complete their current task, authors SHOULD NOT use the assertive value unless the interruption is imperative.

claims.claim: aria-atomic defaults to false and is resolved by walking up the ancestor chain from the changed node: with no explicit ancestor value only the changed node is announced, while aria-atomic="true" causes the entire region including its author-defined label to be re-announced — the difference between hearing "3" and hearing "3 results found".
claims.quote: When the content of a live region changes, user agents SHOULD examine the changed element and traverse the ancestors to find the first element with aria-atomic set […] If none of the ancestors have explicitly set aria-atomic , the default is that aria-atomic is false , and assistive technologies will only present the changed node to the user. […] If aria-atomic is explicitly set to true , assistive technologies will present the entire contents of the element, including the author-defined live region label if one exists.

claims.claim: aria-relevant defaults to "additions text", meaning node removals and text removals are NOT announced by default (a 'foo'→'bar' change announces only 'bar'); the spec tells authors to use removals/all sparingly, and inherited aria-relevant values are overriding rather than additive.
claims.quote: When the aria-relevant attribute is not provided, the default value, additions text , indicates that text modifications and node additions are relevant, but that node removals are irrelevant. […] aria-relevant values of removals or all are to be used sparingly. […] for a text change from 'foo' to 'bar' in a live region with a default aria-relevant value, the text addition ('bar') would be spoken, but the text removal ('foo') would not. […] Although the value is a token list , inherited values are not additive; the value provided on a descendant element completely overrides any inherited value from an ancestor element.

claims.claim: A live region container must already exist in the DOM before content is injected into it; per the ARIA specification the intended behavior is that a live region does NOT announce content it already contains at creation time, only subsequent changes — with role="alert" as the sole exception.
claims.quote: the intended behaviour is **not** to announce any initial content, and to only expose changes/updates – with one exception: containers with `role="alert"`.

claims.claim: role="alert" is specified to behave differently from other live region roles: the user agent fires a system alert event at the moment the alert element is created, which is why a pre-populated role="alert" container announces its initial content while a pre-populated aria-live="polite" or role="status" container does not.
claims.quote: the user agent SHOULD fire a system alert event through the accessibility API _when the WAI-ARIA alert is created_.

claims.claim: The working pattern is prime-then-inject: place (or dynamically create) an EMPTY live region container first, then after a short delay — e.g. a setTimeout — inject the content into it. Creating the container and its content in the same operation fails.
claims.quote: Then, after a short delay (possibly using a `setTimeout()`), you can inject content **into** the live region container.

claims.claim: Announcement presentation of alerts is not uniform across screen readers: NVDA and JAWS prefix the spoken content with the word "Alert", whereas macOS VoiceOver instead plays a non-verbal earcon before the content — so the same markup produces materially different user experiences per screen reader.
claims.quote: NVDA and Jaws will first announce 'Alert', followed by the actual content; in VoiceOver on macOS, alerts are preceded by a special sound/earcon.

claims.claim: Empirical testing across roughly 16 browser/screen-reader combinations (NVDA, JAWS, Narrator, Orca on Chrome/Edge/Firefox; VoiceOver on macOS Safari/Chrome/Firefox and iOS; TalkBack on Android) shows pre-populated live regions generally fail to announce, and support for the pre-populated vs. dynamically-injected cases is highly variable across combinations.
claims.quote: All of these approaches generally fail to produce the desired result

claims.claim: The W3C APG explicitly frames assistive-technology support gaps as a DESIGN-time constraint, instructing that experiences should not be designed to depend on APG pattern features whose must-have behavior support is below 100%.
claims.quote: Where feasible, avoid designing experiences that rely on features of APG patterns that have less than 100% support for must-have behaviors.

claims.claim: Support level is a property of the specific implementation of a pattern, not of the pattern itself: APG states that a sub-100% must-have score for one example implementation does not imply every implementation of that pattern fails the same way, and directs authors to compare support levels across example implementations and to use the pattern's guidelines to design interactions that avoid the problematic features.
claims.quote: If the must-have support level is less than 100% for one example implementation of a pattern, that does not mean every other way of implementing that pattern will present assistive technology users with the same problems.

claims.claim: ARIA-AT scores each tested assistive-technology + browser combination on two measured axes — 'Must-Have Behaviors' (absence can block users entirely) and 'Should-Have Behaviors' (absence impedes users) — giving a quantified, checkable support percentage rather than a binary supported/unsupported verdict.
claims.quote: The assistive technology support tables present two percentages for each assistive technology and browser combination that have been tested: "Must-Have Behaviors" and "Should-Have Behaviors". A behavior designated as "Must-Have" is essential; if not provided, users could be blocked from using the UI element.

claims.claim: Divergent output across screen readers is expected and permitted by the interoperability tests: ARIA-AT does not specify what a screen reader should speak, so identical ARIA can be announced differently by NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver without any of them failing the test.
claims.quote: ARIA-AT interoperability tests do not prescribe exactly how to satisfy a need. For example, they do not specify exactly what a screen reader should speak. Two different screen readers may convey the same information in different ways.

claims.claim: APG warns against the 'code to the bugs' workaround pattern — altering markup to compensate for a specific AT defect — unless the workaround is verified to work both on ATs that lack the bug and after the bug is fixed; this is the APG's own statement of the hazard behind 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA', though that phrase does not appear on this page.
claims.quote:
Avoid modifying code to accommodate an assistive technology bug unless you are confident the modified code provides an experience that:

* Works equally well when using assistive technologies that do not exhibit the bug.
* Will work equally well after the assistive technology bug is fixed.

claims.claim: The APG states that ARIA roles carry no built-in behavior: applying a role does not make browsers supply keyboard handling or styling, so choosing a pattern role obliges the author to implement that role's expected keyboard interactions in JavaScript. This is the mechanism by which pattern choice (disclosure vs tabs, dialog vs alertdialog, etc.) becomes a binding interaction commitment rather than a code annotation.
claims.quote: Is a promise that the author of that <div> has also incorporated JavaScript that provides the keyboard interactions expected for a button. Unlike HTML input elements, ARIA roles do not cause browsers to provide keyboard behaviors or styling. Using a role without fulfilling the promise of that role is similar to making a "Place Order" button that abandons an order and empties the shopping cart.

claims.claim: The APG names concrete cases where ARIA is the wrong answer because it cloaks native semantics: role="log" on a <table> makes assistive technology users no longer perceive a table, and role="navigation" on a <ul> destroys the list container so its <li> children are no longer in a list — an explicit ERROR called out in the guide's own sample code.
claims.quote:
• nav link 1
  • nav link 2

claims.claim: The APG frames ARIA as the rendering layer for the non-visual experience — functionally analogous to CSS for assistive technologies — and states that incorrect ARIA misrepresents the visual experience with potentially devastating effects for screen reader users. This is W3C's stated harm rationale for "No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA" (qualitative; the page gives no measured error rates).
claims.quote: Functionally, ARIA roles, states, and properties are analogous to a CSS for assistive technologies. For screen reader users, ARIA controls the rendering of their non-visual experience. Incorrect ARIA misrepresents visual experiences, with potentially devastating effects on their corresponding non-visual experiences.

claims.claim: aria-label fully replaces, rather than supplements, the element's own content for assistive technology users — the APG's own example shows link text becoming unperceivable once an aria-label is applied. This is a named case where an ARIA attribute silently overwrites information a designer intended to be read.
claims.quote: Link Text

claims.claim: The APG deliberately does not code around browser/assistive-technology support gaps and requires implementers to test every relevant browser + AT combination; examples that misbehave in a given AT are, per W3C, demonstrations of that AT's bugs rather than APG errors. It also states some ARIA features are unsupported in any mobile browser.
claims.quote: Testing assistive technology interoperability is essential before using code from this guide in production. Because the purpose of this guide is to illustrate appropriate use of ARIA 1.2 as defined in the ARIA specification, the design patterns, reference examples, and sample code intentionally do not describe and implement coding techniques for working around problems caused by gaps in support for ARIA 1.2 in browsers and assistive technologies.

result.publishDate: No explicit publish or last-updated date on the page; W3C copyright notice reads 2026. Document is the current ARIA 1.2-era APG \"Read Me First\" practice page.

claims.claim: W3C's First Rule of ARIA states that a native HTML element or attribute with the required semantics and behavior built in must be used in preference to repurposing a generic element and adding an ARIA role/state/property — i.e. ARIA is by rule the fallback, not the default, whenever a native element exists.
claims.quote: If you _can_ use a native HTML element or attribute with the semantics and behavior you require **already built in**, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible**, then do so**.

claims.claim: The Third Rule of ARIA makes keyboard operability a mandatory, author-implemented obligation of choosing an ARIA role: adding role=button to a non-native element requires the author to script focusability and activation via BOTH Enter/Return and Space, because none of that comes with the role.
claims.quote: All interactive ARIA controls must be usable with the keyboard. ... a user must also be able to navigate to the widget and perform an equivalent action using the keyboard ... be able to receive focus and a user must be able to activate the action...using **both** the enter (on WIN OS) or return (MAC OS) and the space key.

claims.claim: The Second Rule forbids overwriting native semantics, and the document gives a concrete wrong/right pair: putting role=tab directly on an <h2> is incorrect; the role must go on a wrapping <div> so the heading semantics survive.
claims.quote:
Do not change native semantics, unless you really have to. ... Do **not** do this: `

heading tab

` Do this: `

heading tab

`

claims.claim: This W3C document contains exactly FOUR rules of ARIA, not five, and contains no statement of the maxim "No ARIA is better than bad ARIA" and no measured-harm data about screen reader users — so the widely cited "five rules of ARIA" and the no-ARIA maxim cannot be sourced to this URL; the document is additionally a Discontinued Draft frozen for historical reference.
claims.quote: Using ARIA is a Discontinued Draft. the four rules of ARIA are kept for historical purposes and for easier reference, but there are no plans to continue work on this document.

claims.claim: The Fourth Rule names a specific wrong use of ARIA: role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" must never be applied to a focusable element (which would leave a keyboard-reachable control with no accessible representation).
claims.quote: Do not use `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on a **focusable** element.

claims.claim: ARIA in HTML makes native element semantics binding at authoring time: authors may use role/aria-* to change an HTML element's exposed meaning, but MUST NOT do so where the ARIA feature conflicts with the element's strong native semantics. Element choice, not later ARIA patching, determines the accessible semantics.
claims.quote: Authors _MAY_ use the ARIA `role` and `aria-*` attributes to change the exposed meaning (semantics) of HTML elements, in accordance with the requirements defined by WAI-ARIA, except where ARIA features conflict with the strong native semantics.

claims.claim: The specification states its own rationale for restricting ARIA: the constraints exist to stop authors from causing assistive technology to report user-interface information that does not correspond to the actual UI. This is the spec-level harm mechanism behind "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" — bad ARIA produces false UI reports to screen reader users, not merely missing information.
claims.quote: Any constraints for the use of ARIA features in HTML defined by this specification are intended to prevent authors from making assistive technology products report nonsensical user interface (UI) information that does not represent the actual UI of the document.

claims.claim: Redundant ARIA roles that merely restate an element's implicit role are explicitly discouraged: role="button" on a native <button> is rated NOT RECOMMENDED. Adding ARIA to an already-correct native element is the wrong answer under this Recommendation even though it looks harmless.
claims.quote: Role=button on `<button>` elements is "NOT RECOMMENDED"

claims.claim: The dialog vs alertdialog distinction is resolved by the element plus one deliberate role override: the HTML <dialog> element carries an implicit role=dialog, alertdialog is the only allowed role change, and explicitly writing role="dialog" on <dialog> is NOT RECOMMENDED. The designer's only ARIA decision in this pattern is "modal" vs "urgent modal".
claims.quote: dialog | role=dialog | Role: alertdialog. (dialog is also allowed, but NOT RECOMMENDED.)

claims.claim: A native <select> with no multiple attribute and no size greater than 1 already maps to role=combobox, so the combobox pattern is obtainable with zero ARIA; building a custom combobox discards a free native mapping and takes on the full ARIA keyboard and state contract.
claims.quote: select (with NO `multiple` attribute and NO `size` attribute having value greater than `1`) | role=combobox

claims.claim: WebAIM states ARIA's first rule is to use a native HTML element or attribute where one exists, and that ARIA applied where HTML already carries the semantics actively creates barriers rather than being merely redundant — i.e. ARIA is the wrong answer whenever a native element covers the semantics.
claims.quote: Rule #1 - If you can use HTML a native HTML element or attribute, then do so. […] When used incorrectly, ARIA can introduce significant accessibility barriers.

claims.claim: Overriding native semantics with a role destroys the element's original semantics: putting role="navigation" directly on a <ul> removes the list semantics, and the correct fix is a structural/markup change (wrap in <div role="navigation">, or use native <nav>) rather than adding ARIA to the list itself.
claims.quote: Rule #2 - Do not change native semantics, unless you really have to.

claims.claim: Choosing an interactive ARIA role is a binding commitment to a keyboard model: every interactive ARIA control must be operable by keyboard, and anything reachable by Tab must also be operable by keyboard activation — so the role choice, made at design time, dictates required keyboard behavior.
claims.quote: Rule #3 - All interactive ARIA controls must be usable with the keyboard. […] If an element is focusable by pressing Tab on the keyboard, it must also be functional—meaning it can respond to keyboard activation.

claims.claim: A live region container carrying aria-live must already be present in the DOM when the page loads; adding the aria-live attribute (or the region) at the moment content is injected is unreliable and will not consistently announce.
claims.quote: This attribute must be set when the page first loads; injecting it later doesn't work reliably.

claims.claim: Semantics-removing ARIA has hard prohibitions tied to focusability: role="presentation" must never be placed on a focusable element, and aria-hidden="true" must never be placed on anything keyboard-navigable — both produce elements a keyboard user can reach but a screen reader cannot describe.
claims.quote: Since `role="presentation"` removes semantics, it must never be applied to a focusable element. […] `aria-hidden="true"` must never be assigned to something that is keyboard-navigable

claims.claim: The APG defines a disclosure as exactly two elements — a trigger button and one section whose visibility it controls — which is the structural commitment that distinguishes it from accordion (multiple coordinated panels) and tabs (mutually exclusive panels sharing one region). Choosing 'disclosure' at design time therefore commits the design to independent, individually-toggled sections with no single-open constraint.
claims.quote: A disclosure is a widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible). It has two elements: a disclosure button and a section of content whose visibility is controlled by the button.

claims.claim: The disclosure pattern obliges a specific and minimal keyboard model: Enter and Space both toggle the control, and no arrow-key navigation is specified. This is the concrete behavioral difference from tabs (arrow-key roving tabindex) and menu/menubar patterns, and it is why a disclosure trigger must be an actual button, not a link or a div.
claims.quote: Enter: activates the disclosure control and toggles the visibility of the disclosure content. Space: activates the disclosure control and toggles the visibility of the disclosure content.

claims.claim: aria-expanded is mandatory on the disclosure trigger and must be kept in sync with visibility state (true when shown, false when hidden), while aria-controls is explicitly optional — so the required design-time deliverable is a visible expanded/collapsed state that the developer can mirror in ARIA, not an ID-wiring decision.
claims.quote: When the content is visible, the element with role `button` has aria-expanded set to `true`. When the content area is hidden, it is set to `false`. ... Optionally, the element with role `button` has a value specified for aria-controls that refers to the element that contains all the content that is shown or hidden.

claims.claim: The APG assigns the visible-state obligation to visual design, not code: the collapsed/expanded state must be communicated by a visual affordance on the button (commonly a right-pointing arrow or triangle when collapsed), meaning the designer must supply a state indicator for the pattern to be implementable as specified.
claims.quote: When the controlled content is hidden, the button is often styled as a typical push button with a right-pointing arrow or triangle to hint that activating the button will display additional content.

claims.claim: The APG's own examples place navigation menus under the disclosure pattern rather than under menu/menubar, evidencing that a site nav dropdown is a disclosure decision (button + aria-expanded, Tab-based traversal) and not an application menu decision (role=menu with arrow-key navigation).
claims.quote: Disclosure (Show/Hide) Navigation Menu ... Disclosure (Show/Hide) Navigation Menu with Top-Level Links

claims.claim: The APG treats disclosure and accordion as two separate named patterns distinguished by content structure — a disclosure governs a single collapsible/expandable region, while an accordion is a vertically stacked SET of interactive headings each owning a section — so choosing between them is a decision about how many sections exist and whether they are headed, not an implementation detail.
claims.quote: A disclosure is a widget that enables content to be either collapsed (hidden) or expanded (visible). ... An accordion is a vertically stacked set of interactive headings that each contain a title, content snippet, or thumbnail representing a section of content.

claims.claim: The APG separates grid from table on the basis of interactivity and keyboard navigation, not visual appearance: a grid is defined by directional-key navigation (arrows, Home, End) among its contents, whereas an ARIA table is explicitly declared static and 'not an interactive widget' — so picking 'grid' commits the design to an arrow-key navigation model.
claims.quote: A grid widget is a container that enables users to navigate the information or interactive elements it contains using directional navigation keys, such as arrow keys, Home, and End. ... Like an HTML table element, a WAI-ARIA table is a static tabular structure containing one or more rows that each contain one or more cells; it is not an interactive widget.

claims.claim: Treegrid is a third, distinct pattern from grid and table, defined by hierarchy plus editability/interactivity of tabular information — meaning the design-time question separating it from grid is whether rows nest and expand, not how the data is styled.
claims.quote: A treegrid widget presents a hierarchical data grid consisting of tabular information that is editable or interactive.

claims.claim: The APG distinguishes alert dialog from modal dialog by communicative intent and required user response rather than by markup: a dialog is defined merely as an overlaid window, while an alert dialog is a modal dialog that interrupts the user's workflow to convey an important message AND acquire a response.
claims.quote: A dialog is a window overlaid on either the primary window or another dialog window. ... An alert dialog is a modal dialog that interrupts the user's workflow to communicate an important message and acquire a response.

claims.claim: The APG distinguishes combobox from listbox by the presence of a text input with an associated popup versus a bare selectable list: combobox is 'an input widget that has an associated popup', while listbox 'presents a list of options' for selecting one or more — so the choice hinges on whether the user types to filter.
claims.quote: A combobox is an input widget that has an associated popup. ... A listbox widget presents a list of options and allows a user to select one or more of them.

claims.claim: Choosing the modal dialog pattern obliges a specific keyboard contract: Tab and Shift+Tab must cycle within the dialog and never move focus outside it, and Escape must close it — a focus trap is a required commitment of the pattern, not an optional enhancement.
claims.quote: Tab: Moves focus to the next tabbable element inside the dialog. If focus is on the last tabbable element inside the dialog, moves focus to the first tabbable element inside the dialog. […] Escape: Closes the dialog. […] Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus outside the dialog. However, unlike most non-modal dialogs, modal dialogs do not provide means for moving keyboard focus outside the dialog window without closing the dialog.

claims.claim: The pattern mandates a two-sided focus-transfer rule: focus moves into the dialog on open, and returns to the invoking element on close (unless that element no longer exists) — making focus origin/destination a design-time decision about which control opens the dialog.
claims.quote: When a dialog opens, focus moves to an element inside the dialog. […] When a dialog closes, focus returns to the element that invoked the dialog unless either: The invoking element no longer exists.

claims.claim: Where initial focus lands is an explicit design decision with content-dependent rules, including deliberately focusing the least destructive action for irreversible operations and adding tabindex="-1" to a static element (e.g. the title or first paragraph) when the dialog content is semantic or long.
claims.quote: add `tabindex="-1"` to a static element at the top of the dialog, such as the dialog title or first paragraph, and initially focus that element […] it may be advisable to set focus on the least destructive action, especially if undoing the action is difficult or impossible […] it may be advisable to set focus to the element that is likely to be most frequently used, such as an OK or Continue button

claims.claim: aria-modal="true" is not a free annotation: applying it can hide outside content from some assistive technologies, so W3C conditions its use on the design actually enforcing modality both behaviorally (no interaction with outside content) and visually (outside content obscured).
claims.quote: marking a dialog modal by setting `aria-modal` to `true` can prevent users of some assistive technologies from perceiving content outside the dialog

claims.claim: Modal dialog and alertdialog are distinct APG patterns selected by purpose, not by implementation convenience: alertdialog is reserved for dialogs that divert attention to a brief, important message, while the generic dialog role covers the overlaid-window case with inert content beneath.
claims.quote: A dialog is a window overlaid on either the primary window or another dialog window. Windows under a modal dialog are inert. […] The alertdialog role is a special-case dialog role designed specifically for dialogs that divert users' attention to a brief, important message.

claims.claim: The APG defines combobox by a design-level distinguisher, not an implementation detail: unlike listbox or menu button, the chosen value is presented in an editable field that the user can select and copy. This is the deciding criterion when a designer picks combobox vs listbox vs a native select.
claims.quote: One feature that distinguishes combobox from both listbox and menu button is that the user's choice can be presented as a value in an editable field, which gives users the ability to select some or all of the value for copying to the clipboard.

claims.claim: Choosing the combobox pattern does not settle the interaction — the designer must additionally choose a popup type, which the APG restricts to exactly four roles (listbox, tree, grid, or dialog), each carrying its own keyboard and structural obligations.
claims.quote: The popup is an element that has role listbox, tree, grid, or dialog.

claims.claim: Combobox obliges a specific, non-obvious focus model: DOM focus never leaves the input while the user navigates the popup; the active option is conveyed only via aria-activedescendant. A design that shows a visually 'focused' option in the list is therefore committing to virtual focus, not real focus.
claims.quote: When a descendant of a listbox, grid, or tree popup is focused, DOM focus remains on the combobox and the combobox has aria-activedescendant set to a value that refers to the focused element within the popup.

claims.claim: The open/closed state of the popup must be exposed programmatically via aria-expanded on the combobox element, mirroring the visible state — so the visual expand/collapse affordance in a design is a binding accessibility commitment, not decoration.
claims.quote: When the combobox popup is not visible, the element with role combobox has aria-expanded set to false. When the popup element is visible, aria-expanded is set to true.

claims.claim: The pattern mandates a specific keyboard contract that separates 'open the popup' from 'move into the popup': Alt+Down Arrow reveals the popup without moving focus, Down Arrow moves focus into it, and Escape dismisses it — three distinct behaviors a design must accommodate once combobox is chosen.
claims.quote: Alt + Down Arrow: If the popup is available but not displayed, displays the popup without moving focus.

claims.claim: Choosing the menu/menubar pattern commits the design to a roving-tabindex keyboard model in which Tab is NOT the intra-widget navigation key — arrow keys move between items and Tab exits the whole widget, so a designer picking 'menu' is picking a keyboard model incompatible with a plain list of tabbable links or buttons.
claims.quote: Tab and Shift + Tab do not move focus among the items in the menu. […] Each item in the menu has `tabindex` set to `-1`, except in a menubar, where the first item has `tabindex` set to `0`.

claims.claim: The menu pattern obliges a specific, non-optional focus-management contract: opening a menu moves focus to its first item, and Escape must close the menu and programmatically return focus to the element that invoked it (menu button or parent menuitem) — focus cannot simply be dropped.
claims.quote: When a menu opens, or when a menubar receives focus, keyboard focus is placed on the first item. […] Escape: Close the menu that contains focus and return focus to the element or context, e.g., menu button or parent `menuitem`, from which the menu was opened.

claims.claim: Any menu item that opens a submenu must expose two separate state/affordance attributes — aria-haspopup (menu or true) and aria-expanded toggled false/true in sync with actual visibility — meaning the design must include a persistent visible 'has submenu' affordance and a visible open/closed state, not just a hover reveal.
claims.quote: A parent menuitem has aria-haspopup set to either menu or true. […] A parent menuitem has aria-expanded set to false when its child menu is not visible and set to true when visible.

claims.claim: Contrary to the widespread claim that ARIA menu roles must never be used for site navigation, the W3C APG menubar page itself ships a navigation menubar example, so the menu-vs-nav decision in APG terms is about committing to the menu keyboard model rather than a blanket prohibition.
claims.quote: Demonstrates a menubar that provides site navigation.

claims.claim: The APG treats a menu opened from a menu button and a menu opened from a menubar as behaviorally identical, so a designer who picks a single dropdown 'menu button' inherits the full menubar keyboard and focus obligations rather than a lighter disclosure model.
claims.quote: Except where noted, menus opened from a menubutton behave the same as menus opened from a menubar.

claims.claim: WebAIM's 2026 automated scan of 1,000,000 home pages found pages containing ARIA averaged 59.1 detected accessibility errors versus 42 on pages with no ARIA — roughly 41% more errors — and the error count scaled with the number of ARIA attributes present.
claims.quote: Home pages with ARIA present had significantly more errors (59.1 on average) than pages without ARIA (42 on average). ... Increased ARIA usage on pages was associated with higher detected errors. The more ARIA attributes that were present, the more detected accessibility errors could be expected.

claims.claim: WebAIM explicitly qualifies the ARIA/error correlation as non-causal, attributing part of the effect to page complexity — so the data supports 'ARIA is a marker of risk' but not the stronger claim that ARIA itself creates the errors.
claims.quote: This does not necessarily mean that ARIA introduced these errors (these pages were also more complex), but pages typically had significantly more errors when more ARIA was present.

claims.claim: The ARIA menu pattern (role="menu") appeared on 5.7% of home pages, and 22% of those implementations actively introduced accessibility barriers because the required menu markup and keyboard interactions were missing — a measured failure rate for one specific APG pattern.
claims.quote: 5.7% of home pages had an ARIA menu (`role="menu"`), but 22% of those ARIA menus introduced accessibility barriers due to the lack of necessary ARIA menu markup and interactions.

claims.claim: ARIA volume on the web is growing fast: 133,589,803 ARIA attributes were detected across the sample, averaging over 133 per page, a 27% increase in one year and more than 6x the 2019 level.
claims.quote: 133,589,803 ARIA attributes were detected—over 133 per page on average! ARIA code increased 27% in just one year and is over 6 times higher than it was in 2019.

claims.claim: Despite heavy ARIA adoption, the dominant WCAG failures remain native-HTML basics solvable without any ARIA — low contrast text (83.9% of pages), missing image alt text (53.1%), missing form input labels (51%), empty links (46.3%), and empty buttons (30.6%) — with 95.9% of pages failing WCAG conformance at 56.1 errors per page.
claims.quote: Home pages averaged 31.4 `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, or `aria-describedby` attributes.

claims.claim: W3C's own authoring guidance asserts the 'No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA' rule on the grounds of concrete harm: incorrect ARIA gives screen reader users a false model of the interface, described as having potentially devastating consequences for the non-visual experience.
claims.quote: Incorrect ARIA misrepresents visual experiences, with potentially devastating effects on their corresponding non-visual experiences.

claims.claim: The APG identifies overriding of native semantics as the specific mechanism of ARIA harm — ARIA acts as a cloak that replaces the original semantics of the element it is placed on, and the guide gives named failure cases (role="log" on a table destroying the exposed table structure; role="navigation" on a list destroying list semantics).
claims.quote: Authors can inadvertently override accessibility semantics.

claims.claim: ARIA is characterized in the APG as simultaneously additive and destructive: the same attribute can enhance an element or erase what a native element already conveyed, which is why the correct answer is often a native element or a layout change rather than an ARIA attribute.
claims.quote: a cloak; it covers up, or overrides, the original semantics or content

claims.claim: The APG disclaims guaranteed assistive-technology support for its own patterns: it requires implementers to test each pattern against every relevant browser + assistive technology combination before production use, and it deliberately does not document workarounds for ARIA 1.2 support gaps, treating such gaps as browser or AT bugs.
claims.quote: Testing assistive technology interoperability is essential before using code from this guide in production. […] It is thus advisable to test implementations thoroughly with each browser and assistive technology combination that is relevant within a target audience.

result.publishDate: No explicit publish or last-updated date on the page; it is a living document carrying "Copyright © 2026 World Wide Web Consortium" (retrieved 2026-07-29). Content corresponds to the ARIA 1.2 era of the APG.

claims.claim: Choosing the ARIA grid pattern over a plain table is a keyboard-model commitment made at design time: a grid is a composite widget that exposes exactly one focusable element to the page tab sequence (roving focus), whereas every focusable element inside a table stays in the tab sequence. The same visual table therefore yields two entirely different keyboard experiences depending on which pattern the designer picks.
claims.quote: A `grid` is a composite widget so it: Always contains multiple focusable elements. Only one of the focusable elements contained by the grid is included in the page tab sequence. … All focusable elements contained in a table are included in the page tab sequence.

claims.claim: Picking grid obliges a specific, non-negotiable arrow-key navigation model — cell-to-cell movement with Right/Left/Up/Down that stops at edges, Home to the first cell in the row, and Control+Home to the first cell of the first row — which is an interaction contract the design must visibly support (visible focus per cell, not per control).
claims.quote: Right Arrow: Moves focus one cell to the right. If focus is on the right-most cell in the row, focus does not move. … Home: moves focus to the first cell in the row that contains focus. … Control + Home: moves focus to the first cell in the first row.

claims.claim: The grid choice carries a documented harm: it puts screen readers into application mode, so users hear only focusable elements and the content labeling them, meaning any non-focusable cell content the designer places in the grid can be silently skipped. This is a concrete case where the more 'ARIA-rich' pattern is the wrong answer for content-heavy tabular data.
claims.quote: While in application mode, a screen reader user hears only focusable elements and content that labels focusable elements. So, screen reader users may unknowingly overlook elements contained in a grid that are either not focusable or not used to label a column or row.

claims.claim: Grid navigation keys are mutually exclusive with in-cell widget keys: while arrow keys are moving cell-to-cell they cannot operate a combobox or move an editing caret, so the pattern requires an explicit mode switch — Enter to disable grid navigation and enter the cell's input, Escape to restore grid navigation. Any cell design containing an arrow-key-driven control forces this extra mode on users.
claims.quote: While navigation keys, such as arrow keys, are moving focus from cell to cell, they are not available to do something like operate a combobox or move an editing caret inside of a cell. … Enter: Disables grid navigation and: If the cell contains editable content, places focus in an input field, such as a textbox. … Escape: restores grid navigation.

claims.claim: The APG constrains grid cell composition to two designs — a cell holding text or a single graphic with focus on the cell, or a cell holding one widget that does not itself need arrow keys with focus on that widget — and states that any grid deviating from these adds complexity for authors, users, or both. Cell content density is therefore a design-time accessibility decision, not a later code fix.
claims.quote: A cell contains text or a single graphic and grid navigation keys set focus on the cell … A cell contains one widget whose operation does not require arrow keys and grid navigation keys set focus on that widget. … grids that do not follow one of these two cell design and focus movement patterns add complexity for authors or users or both.

claims.claim: WebAIM's 2021 Million analysis found home pages using ARIA averaged 41% more detected accessibility errors than pages without ARIA — the quantified harm datapoint for the "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule.
claims.quote: Home pages with ARIA present averaged 41% more detectable errors than those without ARIA.

claims.claim: ARIA is purely descriptive: it changes only what is exposed to assistive technology and adds no behavior, so keyboard handling, focus movement and visible state must be built separately — the design-time commitment a pattern choice creates is not satisfied by adding a role.
claims.quote: It's important to note that ARIA does not add any functionality, it only gives you a way to describe and communicate states or properties to assistive technologies.

claims.claim: Rule 3 of the five rules of ARIA: any interactive ARIA role obliges full keyboard operability equal to the mouse/touch affordance — choosing a widget role is choosing a keyboard model.
claims.quote: all interactive ARIA roles need to be operable by keyboard. If functionality is provided via mouse, touch or any other method of input, it also needs to be available by keyboard.

claims.claim: Composite widget roles (tabs, menu, combobox, grid, tree class of patterns) impose a strict required parent/child role hierarchy and ordering — designers cannot mix roles freely once a composite pattern is chosen.
claims.quote: There is a very strict hierarchy when it comes to composite widgets. These must be composed with very specific Standalone roles, and often in a very specific order. In most cases, you cannot pick and choose which roles you use to compose a widget...

claims.claim: Rule 2 of the five rules: applying an ARIA role to an HTML element overrides that element's native semantics, which is why ARIA is the wrong answer when a native element already carries the semantics (e.g. landmark roles on <header>/<nav>/<main>/<footer>).
claims.quote: When you use an ARIA role on top of HTML, you are explicitly setting the semantics of that element; the ARIA role overrides the HTML semantics.

claims.claim: The canonical W3C "Using ARIA" document codifies FOUR rules of ARIA use, not five, and as of 24 February 2026 it is a Discontinued Draft retained only for historical reference — it explicitly redirects pattern-level guidance to the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG). Any research framing that cites "the five rules of ARIA" as a W3C artifact is citing a non-W3C restatement; the fifth rule (all interactive elements must have accessible names) does not appear in this document.
claims.quote: Using ARIA is a Discontinued Draft. the four rules of ARIA are kept for historical purposes and for easier reference, but there are no plans to continue work on this document. For further guidance on how to include accessibility semantics into web design patterns and widgets using ARIA, see the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG).

claims.claim: The First Rule of ARIA Use makes native HTML the default and ARIA the exception: where a native element already carries both the required semantics AND the required behavior, re-purposing a generic element with an ARIA role is the wrong answer. This is a design-time decision (which control the design commits to) rather than a code fix.
claims.quote: If you *can* use a native HTML element...with the semantics and behavior you require **already built in**, instead of re-purposing an element and adding an ARIA role, state or property to make it accessible**, then do so**.

claims.claim: ARIA supplies semantics only and contributes zero behavior: choosing a non-native element as the base for an interactive widget obliges the team to hand-author BOTH the ARIA semantics and the entire interaction/keyboard model in script. This is the mechanism by which a pattern choice made in design becomes a binding implementation commitment.
claims.quote: If a non-interactive element is used as the basis for an interactive element, developers have to add the semantics using ARIA and the appropriate interaction behavior using scripting.

claims.claim: The Fourth Rule names a concrete, reproducible harm mode of bad ARIA: applying role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" to a focusable element leaves that element still reachable by keyboard but stripped of any announced identity, so screen reader users land on an element that reports nothing.
claims.quote: Do not use `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on a **focusable** element. […] Using either of these on a **focusable** element will result in some users focusing on 'nothing'.

claims.claim: MDN names the specific accessibility failure modes caused by the pre-API SPA transition workaround of keeping old and new views simultaneously in the DOM: lost reading position, focus confusion, and unreliable live region announcements — i.e. the accessibility harm of DIY view transitions is a focus/announcement problem, not a visual one.
claims.quote: Accessibility issues like loss of reading position, focus confusion, and strange live region announcement behavior can also result from having the new and old content both present in the DOM at once.

claims.claim: During a view transition the outgoing view is not live DOM but a static, non-interactive image captured into the ::view-transition-old() pseudo-element, while only ::view-transition-new() represents live content — so anything focusable in the old view ceases to exist as a focus target for the duration of the animation.
claims.quote: ::view-transition-old() — A static snapshot of the old view, before the transition. ::view-transition-new() — A live representation of the new view, after the transition.

claims.claim: The view transition snapshots are painted into a separate overlay pseudo-element tree rooted at ::view-transition that is layered above all other page content, meaning transition visuals sit outside the normal document flow that focus indicators and live regions live in.
claims.quote: ::view-transition — The root of the view transitions overlay, which contains all view transitions and sits over the top of all other page content.

claims.claim: The API splits into two distinct mechanisms — same-document/SPA transitions triggered imperatively by Document.startViewTransition(), and cross-document (MPA) transitions opted into declaratively via the @view-transition CSS at-rule with PageSwapEvent/PageRevealEvent — so an SPA route change must call startViewTransition() around the DOM update itself.
claims.quote: Document.startViewTransition() … Starts a new same-document (SPA) view transition and returns a ViewTransition object to represent it. … In the case of a cross-document navigation, @view-transition is used to opt in the current and destination documents to undergo a view transition.

claims.claim: MDN's View Transition API overview provides no guidance on focus management (where focus should go after the DOM update) and no mention of prefers-reduced-motion — the API itself performs no focus restoration or motion-preference gating, leaving both entirely to the author.
claims.quote: Transitions between states in single-page apps (SPAs) tend to involve writing significant CSS and JavaScript

claims.claim: Deque's stated remedy for SPA client-side view changes is a three-mechanism set — page-title announcement, ARIA live regions, and/or focus management — offered as alternatives rather than a single prescribed behavior; the article never specifies where focus should land on route change, never mentions skip links, and never distinguishes polite from assertive.
claims.quote: Make sure that client-side view changes are known to screen reader users by announcing the change in page title, using ARIA live regions and/or focus management.

claims.claim: Deque frames accessibility as a design-time cost decision: it is cheaper to incorporate starting at UX and Design, and complex or custom interactions should be prototyped early with accessibility included, rather than remediated in code later.
claims.quote: It's easier and less costly to incorporate accessibility the earlier you tackle it, starting with UX and Design.

claims.claim: Deque instructs teams to source widget interaction behavior from the ARIA Authoring Practices rather than inventing custom interaction models — positioning the APG as the catalogue of known patterns to select from.
claims.quote: Check out the ARIA Authoring Practices for known interaction patterns.

claims.claim: Deque asserts semantic HTML structure outranks developer ergonomics, and that framework or CSS tooling choice is not a valid reason to degrade markup semantics — the native-element-first position, though the article does not name any specific ARIA misuse case.
claims.quote: Semantic structure is more important than developer ergonomics. Craft the most semantic HTML pages you can, regardless of your CSS or JavaScript development tools.

claims.claim: Deque recommends questioning whether an SPA or JS framework is needed at all, and where one is used, that core user paths must function with JavaScript disabled via server-side pre-rendering — treating architecture selection as an accessibility decision preceding any focus-management code.
claims.quote: Consider whether a single-page app is really necessary, and if you even need to use a JavaScript framework at all.

claims.claim: In moderated testing of five SPA route-change focus prototypes (5 sessions with NVDA, JAWS, magnification, Dragon voice, and switch access users), moving focus to the new view's heading was the best-performing technique for screen reader users, beating live-region-only and wrapper-focus approaches.
claims.quote: Focusing on a heading was found to be the best experience, as it would save time and make it clear what happened.

claims.claim: Resetting focus to a wrapper element around the whole application on route change — the pattern Gatsby itself shipped via its custom @reach/router implementation — was judged overwhelming in large apps and too subtle to notice compared with heading focus, i.e. the common 'focus the app container' SPA pattern is a documented failure mode.
claims.quote: Focusing on a wrapper element for new content worked okay ... very subtle compared to focusing on a heading.

claims.claim: Focus-management techniques tuned for screen readers actively harmed screen magnification users: full-width focus targets cut off content when zoomed, and for magnification-only users doing nothing on route change was preferable, so the focus target must be a small control (link or icon button), not a large region.
claims.quote: The prototypes pretty much fell apart when zoomed way in

claims.claim: The recommended route-change pattern is a per-view skip link (a real interactive control rendered in each view, visible on keyboard focus) combined with a separate ARIA live region announcing the page name — focus target and announcement deliberately decoupled rather than one element doing both.
claims.quote: Render an interactive UI control in each view that becomes visible when the user navigates through the app by keyboard.

claims.claim: Keyboard-only users could not reach the <main> landmark at all in the tested prototypes because it contained no focusable interactive element, which is why a focusable skip target — not a tabindex="-1" region alone — is required.
claims.quote: users couldn't reach the `<main>` landmark region without focusable interactive elements

claims.claim: ARIA changes only what is exposed to assistive technology; it does not alter browser behavior or visual appearance, so any ARIA pattern chosen at design time obliges the team to separately build the visible state and the keyboard interaction the role implies.
claims.quote: ARIA does not change browser behavior or appearance.

claims.claim: The first of the five rules of ARIA use is to prefer a native HTML element or attribute; WebAIM states explicitly that ARIA used where HTML already carries the semantics, or used incorrectly, creates accessibility barriers rather than removing them.
claims.quote: ARIA should not be used when HTML provides sufficient semantics for accessibility! When used incorrectly, ARIA can introduce significant accessibility barriers.

claims.claim: A concrete named case where ARIA is the wrong answer: putting role="navigation" directly on a <ul> overrides and destroys the list semantics; the correct fixes are a wrapping <div role="navigation"> or, better, the native <nav> element, which needs no ARIA at all.

claims.claim: An aria-live region must already exist in the DOM when the page loads; adding the aria-live attribute at the same time content is injected does not reliably announce.
claims.quote: This attribute must be set when the page first loads; injecting it later doesn't work reliably.

claims.claim: aria-live="polite" queues the update until the screen reader reaches a logical pause and is the default for status/chat/stock updates, while aria-live="assertive" interrupts immediately and should be limited to critical updates such as error messages; role values alert, log and timer also create live regions.
claims.quote: best reserved for critical updates, such as error messages.

claims.claim: As of March 2019 there was no settled best practice among accessibility practitioners for SPA route-change focus: the open questions were whether to move focus to a heading or to a wrapper element, and whether to announce the route change with an ARIA live region at all.
claims.quote: those of us in the community who work with accessibility regularly still can't quite agree on a best practice: should we send focus to a heading, or a wrapper element? Should we announce a page change with ARIA live regions?

claims.claim: Client-side routing removes the browser's built-in accessibility behavior of a page load, so developers must manually manage both keyboard focus and screen reader announcements or AT and keyboard-only users are stranded.
claims.quote: requires developers to manually manage focus and screen reader announcements to ensure assistive technology and keyboard-only users aren't left behind

claims.claim: The two measurable outcomes that distinguish accessible from inaccessible client-side routing are (a) where keyboard focus lands after the route change and (b) what, if anything, the screen reader announces — these were the variables the prototypes isolated.
claims.quote: how keyboard focus is handled with JavaScript: where it leaves a keyboard or screen reader user on the page, and what information (if any) is announced in the screen reader

claims.claim: This page is the study announcement/call for participants only; the actual user-testing results and recommendations were published separately on the Gatsby blog on 2019-07-11, so this URL cannot be cited for empirical findings.
claims.quote: https://www.gatsbyjs.org/blog/2019-07-11-user-testing-accessible-client-routing/

claims.claim: ARIA in HTML is a normative W3C Recommendation that makes specific ARIA usages non-conforming HTML, i.e. bad ARIA is a spec violation and not merely bad practice — named MUST NOT cases include aria-checked on input type=checkbox, aria-checked on input type=radio, and aria-hidden=true on the body element.
claims.quote: Authors _MUST NOT_ use the `aria-checked` attribute on `input type=checkbox` elements. ... authors _MUST NOT_ specify `aria-hidden=true` on the `body` element

claims.claim: The spec names 'overriding interactive elements with non-interactive roles' as a distinct authoring anti-pattern (Section 3.1), i.e. putting a non-interactive ARIA role on a natively interactive element is explicitly called out as against the user's and author's interest.
claims.quote: It is rarely in the user or author's best interest to try and use ARIA to override an interactive element...with a role generally exposed by a non-interactive element.

claims.claim: Native HTML semantics take priority over ARIA by rule: authors may use role/aria-* to change exposed meaning EXCEPT where those features conflict with an element's strong native semantics, and where both native HTML features and ARIA are used the host language feature wins.
claims.quote: Authors _MAY_ use the ARIA `role` and `aria-*` attributes to change the exposed meaning (semantics) of HTML elements, in accordance with the requirements defined by WAI-ARIA, except where ARIA features conflict with the strong native semantics

claims.claim: The W3C states the mechanism of harm from bad ARIA as assistive technology reporting nonsensical UI information to users — this is the spec's own stated rationale for its constraints, though it gives no quantified measurement of that harm.
claims.quote: Any constraints for the use of ARIA features in HTML defined by this specification are intended to prevent authors from making assistive technology products report nonsensical user interface (UI) information

claims.claim: The spec's scope is attribute-level author conformance only — it contains no guidance on live regions/aria-live, focus management on route change, or the APG design patterns (dialog, combobox, tabs), so it cannot serve as a source for research-question topics 1, 3, or 4.
claims.quote: This specification defines the authoring rules (author conformance requirements) for the use of Accessible Rich Internet Applications (WAI-ARIA) 1.2...

claims.claim: W3C's WCAG 2.2 technique ARIA19 states as a hard requirement that the live-region error container must already exist in the DOM at page load — injecting a new element that itself carries role=alert/aria-live will not be announced by most screen readers.
claims.quote: The error container must be present in the DOM on page load for the error message to be spoken by most screen readers.

claims.claim: role=alert is defined by W3C as semantically equivalent to aria-live=assertive, so choosing the role rather than the property is a naming convenience, not a behavioral difference in politeness level.
claims.quote: The following example uses role=alert which is equivalent to using aria-live=assertive .

claims.claim: aria-atomic="true" is documented by W3C as necessary specifically to make VoiceOver on iOS re-announce error messages after more than one invalid submission — a named, screen-reader-specific failure mode when omitted.
claims.quote: aria-atomic=true is necessary to make Voiceover on iOS read the error messages after more than one invalid submission.

claims.claim: Live regions announce content without moving or requiring focus: the AT reads the injected text without the user or the AT focusing the element where the text is displayed, which is why live regions are the mechanism for asynchronous results rather than focus-shifting.
claims.quote: The content within the aria-live region is automatically read by the AT, without the AT having to focus on the place where the text is displayed.

claims.claim: The W3C example prescribes an emptying-then-reinjecting pattern with a 500ms delay before writing new content, explicitly so screen readers notice repeated announcements of the same or similar error text.

claims.claim: The APG tells implementers to treat measured AT support level as a constraint on which pattern is chosen — patterns whose support is below 100% should be approached with caution and, where feasible, experiences should not be designed to depend on those features. This makes the APG's own guidance a design-time gate, not a post-hoc code fix.
claims.quote: Exercise caution when implementing a pattern where support levels are less than 100%.

claims.claim: The APG grades assistive-technology behaviors on a two-level severity scale with a stated user-impact threshold: 'Must-Have' behaviors, whose absence blocks the user from operating the UI element, versus 'Should-Have' behaviors, whose absence merely impedes. This yields a falsifiable per-pattern support percentage rather than a subjective judgement of accessibility.
claims.quote: A behavior designated as 'Must-Have' is essential; if not provided, users could be blocked from using the UI element.

claims.claim: W3C explicitly warns against the common remediation practice of patching markup to work around a specific screen reader's bug, because such a workaround can degrade the experience in assistive technologies that do not have the bug — the mechanism by which well-intentioned ARIA tinkering produces net harm.
claims.quote: Avoid modifying code to accommodate an assistive technology bug unless you are confident the modified code provides an experience that works equally well when using assistive technologies that do not exhibit the bug.

claims.claim: The ARIA-AT interoperability numbers reported in the APG support tables are measured only under each vendor's default assistive-technology configuration, so the published percentages do not describe behavior for users who have customized verbosity or interaction settings.
claims.quote: Unless otherwise noted, all testing is done using the assistive technology vendor's default configuration of an assistive technology.

claims.claim: W3C positions the support tables as a guide that does not substitute for hands-on verification, stating that testing against multiple assistive technologies is a requirement rather than an optional extra — i.e. cross-screen-reader divergence is assumed by the spec authors, not exceptional.
claims.quote: It is essential for all developers to test applications with multiple assistive technologies to ensure a good user experience.

claims.claim: aria-live encodes an interruption policy with exactly three values, defaulting to off: polite defers announcement until the user pauses, assertive cuts into whatever the screen reader is currently saying. This is a design-time decision about how urgent a given async result is, not an implementation detail.
claims.quote: off (default): Changes to the region are not announced / polite: "Assistive technology will wait until the user pauses before announcing updates" / assertive: "Assistive technology will interrupt the user to announce the update"

claims.claim: The live region container must be rendered and present in the DOM before the content is injected into it; creating the region and its content in the same update is contrary to the spec's authoring requirement. This is the single most common cause of silent live regions.
claims.quote: Authors _SHOULD_ create a rendered but empty live region as early as possible (such as on page load), and then modify the content of the live region when the author expects changes to be spoken or brailled.

claims.claim: role=status and role=alert carry implicit aria-live values (polite and assertive respectively), so picking the role IS picking the interruption level — an explicit aria-live attribute is redundant on these roles, and role=alert commits the design to interrupting the user.
claims.quote: role=alert: "A type of live region with important, and usually time-sensitive, information." Implicit `aria-live` value: `assertive` — role=status: Implicit `aria-live` value: `polite`

claims.claim: aria-atomic defaults to false, meaning assistive technology presents only the changed nodes rather than the whole region. A designer specifying "the status line should always be read in full, e.g. '3 of 47 results'" is specifying aria-atomic="true"; without it only the mutated fragment is announced.
claims.quote: aria-atomic: Controls whether assistive technology presents the entire region or only changed nodes. Default value is `false`.

claims.claim: aria-relevant defaults to "additions text", so removals from a live region are not announced by default — a design that communicates state by removing content (clearing a filter chip, dropping a row) is silent to screen reader users unless aria-relevant is changed.
claims.quote: aria-relevant: "Indicates what types of changes have occurred to content within a live region and which changes are relevant." Default value is `"additions text"`.

claims.claim: aria-live has exactly three values whose difference is an interruption-timing commitment, not a styling one: off = no notification, polite = the screen reader waits until the user's current task finishes, assertive = the screen reader interrupts the current task. This is the design-time choice a designer makes when specifying how urgent an async result is.
claims.quote: The aria-live attribute identifies an element as a live region. It takes three possible values: Off (no notification). Polite (screen reader notifies user once current task is complete). Assertive (screen reader interrupts current task to notify user).
